title: compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test always fails since the 1.37 cut: validator ignores MinCompatibilityVersion
content:
**What happened**:

The periodic job [`ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test`](https://prow.k8s.io/?job=ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test) has failed on every run since 2026-08-06 12:48 UTC. The failure rate is 100 percent.

The validator reports one failure:

```
Validating features for emulated_version=1.37, current_version=1.38...
FAIL: feature 'DRAFractionalCapacityRange' expected value 1, got 0
```

The trigger is the release-1.37 branch cut, not a code change. The `v1.37.0-rc.0` tag moved master from `v1.37.0-beta.0` to `v1.38.0-alpha.0`. That shifted the version pair the job validates:

| | Build | Time (UTC) | k/k SHA | Validated pair |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Last green | [2085330939616956416](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416) | 2026-08-06 11:45 | `4f5591ab57b` | emulated 1.36, current 1.37 |
| First red | [2085346290606018560](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560) | 2026-08-06 12:48 | `b882c60b402` | emulated 1.37, current 1.38 |

The commit window holds one commit, `b882c60b402 CHANGELOG: Update directory for v1.37.0-rc.0 release`. It changes only CHANGELOG files, so it is not the cause.

`DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is absent from the `release-1.36` reference list. The job therefore never checked the gate before the cut.

**Root cause**

The kubelet and the control plane report the correct value. The validator expects the wrong one.

`pkg/features/kube_features.go` declares two specs at the same version:

```go
DRAFractionalCapacityRange: {
	{Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
	{Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta, MinCompatibilityVersion: version.MustParse("1.37")},
},
```

`SetEmulationVersion` sets the minimum compatibility version to `emulated - 1`. See `staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go`. The job passes only `--emulated-version=1.37`, so the minimum compatibility version is 1.36. The second spec needs 1.37 or higher. The runtime therefore selects the first spec and reports `0`. This matches the documented behavior of `MinCompatibilityVersion` and the plan in kubernetes/kubernetes#140594, which schedules the on-by-default promotion for 1.38.

Two problems in the tooling make the validator disagree:

1. The generator `test/compatibility_lifecycle/cmd/feature_gates.go` in kubernetes/kubernetes does not write `minCompatibilityVersion` into `versioned_feature_list.yaml`. In that file the two specs differ only in `default`, so no consumer can tell them apart.

   ```yaml
   - name: DRAFractionalCapacityRange
     versionedSpecs:
     - default: false
       lockToDefault: false
       preRelease: Beta
       version: "1.37"
     - default: true
       lockToDefault: false
       preRelease: Beta
       version: "1.37"
   ```

2. `get_target_spec` in `experiment/compatibility-versions/versioned_specs_util.sh` takes `last` of the matching specs. It selects the `default: true` spec and expects `1`.

`DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is the only feature in kubernetes/kubernetes that uses `MinCompatibilityVersion`. That is why the problem appears now.

**What you expected to happen**:

The job passes. The validator selects the spec that applies at the minimum compatibility version the job actually runs with.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

```bash
SPECS='[{"default":false,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"},
        {"default":true,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}]'

# current get_target_spec behavior
echo "$SPECS" | jq -r --arg ver 1.37 \
  '[ .[] | select((.version|tonumber) <= ($ver|tonumber)) ] | last | .default'
# => true   (validator expects 1)

# what the control plane reports at --emulated-version=1.37
# kubernetes_feature_enabled{name="DRAFractionalCapacityRange",stage="BETA"} 0
```

**Please provide links to example occurrences, if any**:

- First red build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560
- Last green build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416
- TestGrid tab: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-api-machinery-emulated-version#compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test

Of the 229 builds still in GCS, 150 passed and 79 failed. Every pass is before the boundary. Every failure is after it. No build interleaves, so this is not a flake.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Control that isolates the cause.** The job `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test-n-2` runs the same validator against the same master build, but it validates emulated 1.36 against current 1.38. It stays green. The break is specific to the 1.37 spec pair.

**Suggested fix, in two parts.**

Part 1 clears CI. Change `get_target_spec` to take the first spec at the highest matching version instead of the last. That selects the spec that applies at the default minimum compatibility version.

```jq
[ .[] | select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) <= ($ver|sub("^v";"")|tonumber)) ] as $c
| ($c | map(.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) | max) as $m
| ($c | map(select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) == $m)) | first)
```

I checked this against normal features at 1.31, 1.33 and 1.35. The result does not change. The result changes only when two specs share a version.

This part is necessary, not only convenient. The `release-1.37` reference list is frozen. It will never carry `minCompatibilityVersion`. The validator must therefore fall back to first-wins for the 1.37 pair whatever else changes.

Part 2 prevents the next occurrence. Write `minCompatibilityVersion` from the kubernetes/kubernetes generator, then compare against it in the validator for 1.38 and later.

**Related.** This validator has missed a feature gate lifecycle pattern twice before. See kubernetes/test-infra#34396 and kubernetes/test-infra#35179. Expect the problem to return at the 1.38 cut if the gate is promoted per kubernetes/kubernetes#140594 without matching validator work.

Owner is SIG API Machinery. The alert address on the job is `compatibility-version-test@google.com`. Feature owners are @sunya-ch and @pohly.


---

/transfer kubernetes

Trying to get up to speed with what this test is doing and what is failing:
* Running against master (e.g. `gitVersion v1.38.0-alpha.0.10+a76f2bbb5a67c4`)
* Detecting to be alpha.0, so *trying* to act like the previous minor (1.37) ([link](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/65ee596273d3043e0e307e54405bc31470d63d3c/experiment/compatibility-versions/compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test.sh#L195-L206)), but I'm unsure whether the way it's doing this is correct (setting VERSION_DELTA to -2?)
* Running a cluster with current version = 1.38, emulated version = 1.37 and scraping feature enablement metrics

to debug this script, here was my setup:
```sh

# setup
git clone https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra.git
git clone https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes.git
cd kubernetes

# extract feature yamls
git show upstream/release-1.37:./test/compatibility_lifecycle/reference/versioned_feature_list.yaml > ~/tmp/feature-1.37.yaml
git show upstream/master:./test/compatibility_lifecycle/reference/versioned_feature_list.yaml > ~/tmp/feature-master.yaml
# copy latest_metrics.txt from failed run artifacts to ~/tmp/latest_metrics.txt

# run
../test-infra/experiment/compatibility-versions/validate-compatibility-versions-feature-gates.sh 1.37 1.38 ~/tmp/latest_metrics.txt ~/tmp/feature-master.yaml ~/tmp/feature-1.37.yaml ~/tmp/results.txt
```

with the same failed results:
```
more ~/tmp/results.txt 
FAIL: feature 'DRAFractionalCapacityRange' expected value 1, got 0
```

To resolve this, we need to:
1. add `minCompatibilityVersion` info into the feature yaml published from k/k (master PR in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141324, will auto-fast-forward to release-1.37)
2. take that into account in the script used in this test (PR in https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37665)

/sig architecture

Once the [fix](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141324) is [auto-fast-forwarded](https://prow.k8s.io/?job=ci-fast-forward) to [release-1.37](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commits/release-1.37/), the [next run](https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test) should be green

job is green

/close

@liggitt: Closing this issue.

<details>

In response to [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141283#issuecomment-5267363154):

>job is green
>
>/close

/sig scheduling 🤖 let's figure out why TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin is flaky here: https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin#ec8292b640cdf40198e4 ## `TestPodGroupScheduling` / `TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin` — triage (revised) **Verdict: recent scheduler regression — not a timing flake, and not an arch/emulation issue.** A clean onset on **2026-06-26** that hits *both* native amd64 and arm64. Leading suspect: **#139602** (`scheduler: Add resourceVersion to Pod status patch`, merged 2026-06-26 16:26 UTC). > Correcting an earlier take on this thread: these integration jobs do **not** run under QEMU. arm64 pins `nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/arch: arm64` (real hardware), and s390x/ppc64le run on dedicated `k8s-infra-{s390x,ppc64le}-prow-build` clusters. "Slow emulated arch" is not the cause. ### Evidence **Shared signature** — a timeout, not an assertion mismatch: ``` --- FAIL: TestPodGroupScheduling/gang_pods_are_unschedulable_due_to_lack_of_space ... error: context deadline exceeded --- FAIL: TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin/... (~30s) ``` [Triage cluster `ec8292b640cdf40198e4`](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin#ec8292b640cdf40198e4) **Clean onset on arm64.** The permit/gang cluster (`TestPodGroupScheduling`, `TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin`, `TestUnReservePreBindPlugins`) did not fail **once** in the ~800 builds from 05-30 → 06-26 16:xx. It appears immediately after #139602 merged: | arm64 build day | permit/gang-cluster failures | |---|---| | 05-30 → 06-26 15:xx | **0** — prior reds were unrelated (`TestDRA`, `TestAsyncPreemption`, JWT, apiserver…), a different test each time = real background noise | | 06-26 (after 16:26 merge) | 1 — first-ever `TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin` @ 23:01 ([build](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-integration-arm64-master/2070643583718789120)) | | 06-27 / 06-28 | 1 / 3 | | 06-29 → 07-01 | 4 → ~9 → ~7 (`TestPodGroupScheduling` on nearly every run) | **Not arch-specific.** Native amd64 `ci-kubernetes-integration-master` was **0/16 on 06-25**, then began failing the *same* tests from 06-27 (`TestUnReservePreBindPlugins`, `TestCoSchedulingWithPermitPlugin`, `TestPodGroupScheduling`). `-race` (slow amd64) too. Same tests failing across independent architectures right after the same merge ⇒ code regression, not environment; arm64/`-race` just hit it at a higher rate because they're slower. ### Root cause (suspect) **#139602** is the *only* `pkg/scheduler` change in the 06-25 → 06-27 window, landing ~6.5 h before the first failure. It adds `metadata.resourceVersion` to the scheduler's pod-status patches ([`util.PatchPodStatus`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go), [`pod_status_patch.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/api_calls/pod_status_patch.go)) so async-bind conflicts can be detected: ```go newPod := v1.Pod{Status: *newStatus} if resourceVersion != "" { newPod.ResourceVersion = resourceVersion // patch now 409-conflicts on a stale cache } ``` Before this PR the status patch carried no resourceVersion and *could not* conflict. Now, when the scheduler's cached pod is stale, the patch fails with `Operation cannot be fulfilled on pods … the object has been modified`, the pod's `PodScheduled=False` / gang status never converges, and a test polling for "unschedulable" exhausts its 30 s deadline → `context deadline exceeded`. Genuine binding conflicts are present in the failing logs (`Operation cannot be fulfilled on pods/binding`). More contention on slower arches → more stale-cache conflicts → higher failure rate, which is why arm64 surfaced it first. ### Suggested next step Confirm by reverting #139602 (or its `PatchPodStatus` resourceVersion path) and re-running the scheduler integration suite. If confirmed, the fix belongs in the scheduler's conflict handling (re-fetch + retry on 409) — **not** in widening the test timeout, which would only mask patches that never succeed. /cc @nojnhuh ### Prior art - The same test flaked years ago under genuine timing pressure: #88469 (closed) — a different root cause from this regression. - Suspect PR: #139602. /sig scheduling /kind failing-test /kind regression --- *🔬 Automated triage on behalf of @dims, generated by Claude with the `k8s-ci-triage` skill. May contain mistakes — verify before acting.* It looks like #139602 is the cause. I'm closing in on a fix to narrow the scope of that change. /assign I opened #140177 which reduces the impact of #139602 to cover only the cases observed in #139417 and restores the previous behavior in the case this test is hitting. cc @macsko Fixed by #140911 /close @nojnhuh: Closing this issue.

title: Flaky test: TestValidateEvictionStatusUpdate/mark_active_and_started on Windows
content:
### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Which tests are flaking?

TestValidateEvictionStatusUpdate/mark_active_and_started

### Since when has it been flaking?

Since commit `fc558fb4e9fa9da1dc583f5c71f27cd54debc4ae` — "introduce EvictionRequest and Eviction API" (merged 2026-07-23). This commit introduced the `TestValidateEvictionStatusUpdate` test along with the "mark active and started" case, which from the start used `metav1.Now()` vs `clock.Now()` non-deterministically.

### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140855/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080738822861099008

### Reason for failure (if possible)

In the "mark active and started" test case, `oldInput` (`mkValidEvictionStatus(2)`) sets `Responders[0].StartTime` to `metav1.Now()` (wall clock), while `input` overrides it with `clock.Now()` (fake clock initialized from `time.Now()`). On Windows, the system clock resolution is ~15ms, so both calls can return the same timestamp. When that happens, `SemanticDeepEqual` considers `oldInput` and `input` equal, triggering the "Expected oldInput and input to differ" assertion (line 816).

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig windows

title: [Bug] Non-admin users can self-escalate to DRA device adminAccess by labeling their own namespace (no RBAC check on the capability itself)
content:
**TL;DR:** requesting `adminAccess: true` on a DRA device request only checks whether the containing
namespace carries the label `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true`. It does **not** check whether the
*creating principal* has any elevated permission. `DRAAdminAccess` is GA and locked-on by default since v1.36,
so this is the live behavior of any stock cluster today.

**Self-escalation, verified live (details withheld here — see note at the end).** A principal holding only:
- ordinary `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` (needed to use DRA at
  all), and
- `get`/`patch` on exactly *one* `Namespace` object, by name, via `resourceNames` — a narrow, realistic
  self-service pattern many platforms grant so app teams can manage their own namespace's labels/annotations
  (chargeback tags, network-policy selectors, etc.), confirmed via `kubectl auth can-i` to grant **no**
  access to any other namespace and **no** unscoped `namespaces` access,

was able to label its own namespace with `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` and immediately have a
`ResourceClaim` with `adminAccess: true` accepted — a claim that had been rejected moments earlier with the
identical spec, before the namespace was labeled. No cluster-admin, no cluster-wide `namespaces` access, no
help from any other actor. This user granted *themselves* a capability that "ignores all ordinary claims to
the device with respect to access modes" (direct quote from the field's own doc comment), using a permission
scope that has nothing to do with device access and that many clusters already hand out for unrelated
self-service reasons.

**Baseline confirmation (no elevated permission of any kind).** Before the self-escalation test above, the
same claim was tried with *zero* `namespaces` access at all: a `ServiceAccount` bound to a `Role` granting
only ordinary `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` — successfully
created the identical `adminAccess: true` claim in a namespace someone else had already labeled, and was
rejected with the exact same spec in an otherwise identical, unlabeled namespace:

| Namespace | Principal's RBAC | `adminAccess: true` claim |
|---|---|---|
| `admin-labeled` (pre-labeled by someone else) | create/get/list/watch/delete on `resourceclaims` only | **Created successfully** |
| `admin-unlabeled` (no label) | identical | Rejected: `Forbidden: admin access to devices requires the ` `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` ` label on the containing namespace` |
| `admin-unlabeled`, **after** the same principal is given narrow self-service `get`/`patch` on just that one namespace and labels it themselves | unchanged claim-related RBAC, +self-service namespace-metadata edit only | **Created successfully — self-escalation** |

**Contrast with the two other authorization checks in the same file.** `pkg/registry/resource/utils.go`
contains three related checks. Two of them go through the real authorizer against a dedicated synthetic
subresource:

```go
// AuthorizedForBinding checks if the caller is authorized to update
// status.allocation and status.reservedFor by verifying permission on the
// synthetic resourceclaims/binding subresource.
func AuthorizedForBinding(ctx context.Context, fieldPath *field.Path, authz authorizer.Authorizer, ...) field.ErrorList {
    ...
    attrs := &syntheticSubresourceAttrs{
        Attributes:  baseAttrs,
        subresource: resourcev1.SubresourceBinding,
        ...
    }
    if err := checkAuthorization(ctx, authz, attrs); err != nil { ... }
}
```

`AuthorizedForDeviceStatus` follows the same pattern against a `resourceclaims/driver`-style subresource. The
third — `AuthorizedForAdmin` — does not:

```go
// AuthorizedForAdmin checks if the request is authorized to get admin access to devices
// based on namespace label
func AuthorizedForAdmin(ctx context.Context, deviceRequests []resource.DeviceRequest, namespaceName string, nsClient v1.NamespaceInterface) field.ErrorList {
    ...
    ns, err := nsClient.Get(ctx, namespaceName, metav1.GetOptions{})
    ...
    if ns.Labels[resource.DRAAdminNamespaceLabelKey] != "true" {
        return append(allErrs, field.Forbidden(adminAccessPath, ...))
    }
    return allErrs
}
```

No `authorizer.Authorizer` call, no synthetic subresource — just a label read.

### What did you expect to happen?

One of two things, either of which would close this gap:

- `adminAccess` is gated the same way `binding`/`driver` status updates already are — a real RBAC check
  against a dedicated synthetic subresource (e.g. `resourceclaims/adminaccess`), so a cluster operator can
  scope *who* is allowed to request it independently of namespace labeling; or
- if the namespace-label design is intentional (e.g. because whoever can label a namespace is assumed to
  already be a namespace-level admin), that assumption does not hold up — see "Self-escalation" above.
  Ordinary `get`/`patch` on *one's own* `Namespace` object, scoped via `resourceNames` (a narrow self-service
  pattern, not "namespace-level admin" in any broad sense), is sufficient to set the label and immediately
  self-grant `adminAccess`. If the label-based design is kept, setting this *specific* label should require a
  permission distinct from ordinary namespace-metadata editing (which RBAC cannot currently express, since
  `namespaces` `patch`/`update` has no per-label-key granularity) — which argues for moving the check to a
  real subresource-based authorization instead.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducible deterministically on any `kind` cluster running v1.36+ with `DynamicResourceAllocation` and a
`DeviceClass` available (no real hardware or even a functioning driver required — this check happens at
`ResourceClaim` admission time, before any scheduling/allocation is attempted). General shape (exact manifests
and command transcript intentionally not included here — see closing note):

1. Two otherwise-identical namespaces, only one carrying `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true`.
2. An ordinary principal in each namespace, granted only `create/get/list/watch/delete` on
   `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` — confirmed via `kubectl auth can-i` to have no other permission
   (no `namespaces` access, no access to the real RBAC-protected `resourceclaims/binding` or
   `resourceclaims/status` subresources).
3. The identical `adminAccess: true` `ResourceClaim` attempted by that principal in both namespaces — succeeds
   only in the labeled one, confirming the label (not any RBAC permission) is the sole gate.
4. Follow-up: that same principal is then granted exactly one additional, narrow permission — `get`/`patch`
   on *only its own* `Namespace` object, by name — confirmed via `can-i` to grant nothing else (not access to
   any other namespace, not unscoped `namespaces` access). Using only that permission, the principal labels
   its own namespace and immediately passes the same check that had just rejected it — full self-escalation,
   with no cluster-admin or cluster-wide `namespaces` access involved anywhere.

This reproduces every time, has no timing dependency, and does not depend on the specific DRA driver used
(verified with a public example driver simulating GPUs — no real hardware needed).

**Sample output showing the baseline rejection (safe to share, does not enable exploitation on its own):**

```
$ kubectl -n admin-unlabeled apply -f claim.yaml --as=<ordinary-principal-with-no-namespaces-access>
The ResourceClaim "admin-claim" is invalid: spec.devices.requests[0].adminAccess: Forbidden: admin access to
devices requires the `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` label on the containing namespace
```

The full transcript showing the subsequent self-escalation (labeling the namespace, then the same claim
succeeding) is withheld from this public issue — see the note at the end.

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`;
live-verified on `kindest/node:v1.36.1`.

**1. `AuthorizedForAdmin`** (`pkg/registry/resource/utils.go`) — the check under discussion, shown in full
above. Invoked from `resourceclaimStrategy.Validate` on every `ResourceClaim` create
(`pkg/registry/resource/resourceclaim/strategy.go`) and the equivalent path for `ResourceClaimTemplate`.

**2. `AuthorizedForBinding` and `AuthorizedForDeviceStatus`**, same file — both go through
`authorizer.Authorizer` against a dedicated synthetic subresource (`resourceclaims/binding`,
`resourceclaims/driver`-style attributes respectively). These are the pattern `AuthorizedForAdmin` doesn't
follow.

**3. `DRAAdminAccess` feature-gate history** (`pkg/features/kube_features.go`):

```go
DRAAdminAccess: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.32"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.34"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.GA, LockToDefault: true}, // GA in 1.36; remove in 1.39
},
```

GA and `LockToDefault: true` since v1.36 — this is the permanent, non-optional behavior of the API going
forward, not something a cluster operator can currently disable even if they wanted to while a fix lands.

**4. What `adminAccess` actually grants**, per its own doc comment (`pkg/apis/resource/types.go`): it "ignores
all ordinary claims to the device with respect to access modes" — i.e. it's explicitly a
privilege-escalation-shaped capability (bypassing normal exclusivity/access restrictions on a device), which
is exactly the kind of thing the project already has a pattern (`AuthorizedForBinding`/`AuthorizedForDeviceStatus`)
for gating properly.

**5. Defaulting itself is safe** — `AdminAccess` is a `*bool`; unset/false means disabled, so there's no
fail-open default. The gap is specifically in the enforcement mechanism for the "true" case.

### Why this matters in practice

Two distinct real-world paths to the same outcome, in increasing order of how deliberate they need to be:

1. **Self-escalation (verified live above, the more serious path).** Any user with the narrow, common
   self-service permission to edit their own namespace's metadata — a pattern many platforms grant precisely
   so app teams don't need a ticket to add their own labels/annotations — can grant *themselves*
   `adminAccess` on demand, with zero involvement from any other actor. To be precise about what this
   permission is *not*: it isn't equivalent to cluster-admin or even namespace-admin — it grants nothing
   beyond editing metadata on that one `Namespace` object. But it is fair to say that, given this bug,
   granting it implicitly and silently also grants the DRA `adminAccess` capability for that namespace — a
   completely separate, undocumented capability the grantor never chose to hand out and most likely doesn't
   know exists. RBAC gives the grantor no way to decouple "edit your own namespace's labels" from "grant DRA
   device-privilege bypass in that namespace," since there is no per-label-key permission to withhold just
   the one label that matters.

2. **Incidental exposure via unrelated automation.** The namespace label is otherwise settable by anyone with
   plain `namespaces` `update`/`patch` RBAC, which in real clusters is often held more broadly still — GitOps
   reconcilers, PSA/Istio sidecar-injection automation — none of whom are necessarily making a considered
   decision to grant every current and future claim-creator in that namespace a device-privilege-escalation
   capability. Once labeled for any reason (including an unrelated automation reusing the same key by
   coincidence, or a namespace labeled once and never revisited), every principal with ordinary claim-create
   rights in that namespace silently gains `adminAccess` with no further signal, audit trail, or independent
   permission check.

Path 1 is the one to lead with when discussing severity — it doesn't require any misconfiguration or
carelessness, just a permission grant that is common, reasonable, and completely unrelated to device access
on its face.

### A note on what's not included here

The exact RBAC manifests and full `kubectl` command transcript that demonstrate the self-escalation
end-to-end have intentionally been left out of this public issue, to avoid publishing a ready-to-run
privilege-escalation script while this is unpatched. Everything needed to understand, locate, and fix the
underlying gap is above. Happy to provide the full reproduction (manifests + transcript) privately — already
shared with security@kubernetes.io — to any SIG Auth/SIG Node approver or Security Response Committee member
working this issue; just ask.

### Kubernetes version

<details>
Live reproduction: `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream via `kind`. Code paths involved confirmed
identical at tag `v1.36.3` (latest stable at time of this report) and master HEAD
`94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f` by direct source comparison. `DRAAdminAccess` is GA since v1.36.
</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
None — plain `kind` (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster.
</details>

### OS version

<details>
Whatever the `kind` node image ships (containerized, not relevant to this bug).
</details>

### Install tools

<details>
`kind` v0.32.0.
</details>

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd (as shipped in the `kind` node image).
</details>

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
A public example DRA driver (kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) — used only to provide a real
`DeviceClass` for the claim to reference. Not specific to this driver: the check under discussion runs
entirely in `kube-apiserver`'s registry/admission code, before any driver involvement, and would reproduce
identically with any DRA driver or even a `DeviceClass` with no working driver at all.
</details>

As mentioned on slack to @peppi-lotta, this is not a blocker for 1.37 release, although it's an actual problem in the test. Specifically, after updating the image from a broken to a new one, we only wait for status generation to catch up, but we're not waiting for pods, see here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f/test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go#L1451-L1454 and compare that with initial rollout a few lines before: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f/test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go#L1414-L1418

Fix is in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141292

title: Single instance deployment will be unavailable during eviction
content:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
When the pod is evicted, the service is unavailable.
```
NAME         ENDPOINTS           AGE
echoserver   10.244.1.219:8080   176m
echoserver   <none>   178m
echoserver   10.244.3.219:8080   178m
```
If use `PodDisruptionBudget`, Pod can't be evicte.
```
error when evicting pod "echoserver-55c6c59dd5-kg4p4" (will retry after 5s): Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.
evicting pod echoserver/echoserver-55c6c59dd5-kg4p4
```

**What you expected to happen**:
* When voluntary disruptions occur, old pods should not be evicted from the `Endpoints`  immediately until the new pod is available.
* If there is only one replicas, Pods should be allowed to be evicted until a new Pod is successfully created and ready.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
deploy resource:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: echoserver
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: echoserver
  namespace: echoserver
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: echoserver
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: echoserver
    spec:
      containers:
        - image: gcr.io/google_containers/echoserver:1.0
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          name: echoserver
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: echoserver
  namespace: echoserver
spec:
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      protocol: TCP
  selector:
    app: echoserver
  type: NodePort
---
apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: echoserver
  namespace: echoserver
spec:
  # minAvailable: 1
  maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: echoserver
```
then `kubectl drain node`

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"18", GitVersion:"v1.18.1", GitCommit:"7879fc12a63337efff607952a323df90cdc7a335", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-04-08T17:38:50Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.9", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"18", GitVersion:"v1.18.2", GitCommit:"52c56ce7a8272c798dbc29846288d7cd9fbae032", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-04-16T11:48:36Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.9", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
- Install tools:
kubeadm
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:


---

/sig apps

The documentation for maxUnavailable says "one can prevent all voluntary evictions by specifying 0." From my understanding, that policy blocking node drain is working as designed.

Is there currently a way to keep stateless single instances  serivce avaliable when they are evicted?

No, the removal of one pod is the signal to spin up another instance. A replica count of 2 is required to allow eviction without interruption. 

Do we need to consider a solution to keep the stateless single instances service available?
Involuntary disruptions make single-instance services unavailable. I think it is reasonable. Should voluntary disruptions consider the availability of single-instance services?
I know that the guarantee level of the single instance service is not high, but I still want to serivce keep available when being voluntary disruptions evicted.
In my case, it makes the cluster defragment and compact nodes complicated.

If you want to keep the pod available, set a longer termination grace period and delay shutdown in your process.  You will be removed from serving rotations, but your process will still be alive.

> If you want to keep the pod available, set a longer termination grace period and delay shutdown in your process. You will be removed from serving rotations, but your process will still be alive.

It seems that the eviction started, the pod was removed from the endpoints?

I just saw this one after finding also https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48307, it seems that's the same behavior you get when you delete a pod, it's removed from service/endpoints as soon as the delete command is executed, even if at the same time another pod is started to meet with the replica count.

Having the ability to do a graceful drain (similar to a rolling deploy) for deployments with only one replica would be very nice to have, especially since it's a voluntary action, obviously this can't be the case for involuntary events.

In our use case we have a lot of non production services and a very dynamic infrastructure (instances go up and down all the time since we use spot instances) so we have a few downtimes a day unless we decide to use at least 2 replicas for each deployment. That will basically defeat the purpose of spot instances, if we save 60-65% by using them and we then have to run twice the pods to compensate the drains downtime there would be almost no savings. There's really no way this can be ever considered in the future @liggitt ?

It's a pity that it is still not addressed, especially since `kubectl rollout restart` is perfectly able to restart even single-replica Deployments in a graceful non-disruptive way.

@alex88 @shapirus did you manage to find a solution or workaround to this issue? I am in the exact same situation and revisited PDB documentation in hope of finding something new.

> @alex88 @shapirus did you manage to find a solution or workaround to this issue? I am in the exact same situation and revisited PDB documentation in hope of finding something new.

Unfortunately, I totally fail to recall what I ended up with on this one. I might have scaled the more critical apps to 2 pods or something. Not sure, sorry. But please comment here if you find something :).

@liggitt , don't think it's fair to close this ticket, this is not about PDB but it's about being able to having single HA pod per deployment for non-production workload or spot instances.

If you propose to have two replicas, Imagine if I have an application with 600 MB of memory, 500 MB bootstrapping resources and 100 for the actual end user load in nonprod, do you see it's just to have two replicas with total 1200 MB for each deployment of such just to provide HA during the eviction?


If you propose to set PDB, we are already talking about single pod per deployment so that the cost matters, having PDB that prevents draining a node with single pod means a node will be up all the time serving 1 pod which can't be evicted.

Sorry for necroposting, but since this issue is still unaddressed, I'd like to say there is now a tool that closes this gap exactly: https://github.com/kylan11/understudy

title: ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery testing should allow any supported algorithm
content:
### What happened?

We switched to using ES384 and ran into an issue with conformance testing where the ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery testcase failed.

```
[FAIL] [sig-auth] ServiceAccounts ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery should support OIDC discovery of service account issuer [Conformance]

Pod logs:
OK: Got token
validating with in-cluster discovery
OK: got issuer https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local/
failed to validate with in-cluster discovery: oidc: id token signed with unsupported algorithm, expected ["RS256" "ES256"] got "ES384"
```


### What did you expect to happen?

The testcase should not be more restrictive than the actual cluster code.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable ES384 and run the test.

### Anything else we need to know?

It seems the ServiceAccountIssuerDiscovery testcase only allows RS256 or ES256:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7ed622c80f39f99dc9efc8275fd1244b1791fa67/test/images/agnhost/openidmetadata/openidmetadata.go#L126-L128

But the actual code allows additional algorithms:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/serviceaccount/externaljwt/plugin/plugin.go#L177-L180

It would probably make sense to update the testcase to align with the supported algorithms.

title: Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles CoreDNS v1.13.1 — 3 minor versions behind upstream v1.14.6, exposing clusters to 49+ known CVEs
content:
## Summary

Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles `registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1` as the
default DNS provider. The upstream CoreDNS project has since released v1.14.6,
which addresses the vast majority of known vulnerabilities present in v1.13.1.

Since Kubernetes controls which CoreDNS version ships with each release, and
cluster administrators rely on the officially bundled version, we are requesting
that the CoreDNS version be bumped in an upcoming Kubernetes patch release.

/sig network
/area dns
/kind bug
/priority important-soon

## Environment

- **Kubernetes Version:** v1.35.1
- **Bundled CoreDNS:** registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1
- **Latest Upstream CoreDNS:** v1.14.6
- **OS:** Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.0 (Coughlan)
- **Scanners:** Dependency-Track, Trivy

## Why This Matters

Cluster administrators installing Kubernetes v1.35.1 via kubeadm or other
official tooling receive CoreDNS v1.13.1 by default. Most organizations
rely on the officially bundled versions and do not independently upgrade
individual control plane components.

While it is technically possible to manually upgrade CoreDNS to v1.14.6,
this is:
- Not documented as a supported configuration for v1.35.1
- A burden on every individual cluster administrator rather than a fix at source

## Vulnerability Comparison: v1.13.1 vs v1.14.6

We scanned both versions to quantify the security impact.

### Dependency CVEs

| Dependency | v1.13.1 Version | v1.14.6 Version | CVEs in v1.13.1 | CVEs in v1.14.6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| golang.org/x/crypto | 0.42.0 | 0.53.0 | 32 (7 Critical) | 1 (Unknown) |
| golang.org/x/net | 0.45.0 | (newer) | 8 | 0 |
| google.golang.org/grpc | 1.75.1 | 1.82.0 | 2 (1 Critical) | 1 (High) |
| github.com/quic-go/quic-go | 0.55.0 | (newer) | 4 | 0 |
| github.com/expr-lang/expr | 1.17.6 | (newer) | 2 | 0 |
| golang.org/x/sys | 0.36.0 | (newer) | 1 | 0 |
| **Total** | | | **49** | **2** |

### CoreDNS-Specific CVEs Fixed Between v1.13.1 and v1.14.6

| CVE | Severity | Fixed In | Description |
|-----|----------|----------|-------------|
| CVE-2026-26017 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DNS access control bypass due to plugin execution order |
| CVE-2026-26018 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DoS via predictable PRNG |
| CVE-2026-32934 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS due to unbounded resource growth |
| CVE-2026-32936 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS via oversized DNS-over-HTTPS GET requests |
| CVE-2026-33190 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Auth bypass via flawed TSIG plugin verification |
| CVE-2026-33489 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Info disclosure via incorrect ACL stanza selection |
| CVE-2026-35579 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Auth bypass for TSIG-protected functionalities |
| CVE-2025-68151 | MEDIUM | 1.14.0 | DoS via unbounded connections |
| CVE-2025-47950 | HIGH | 1.12.2 | DoQ Memory Exhaustion |
| CVE-2023-28452 | HIGH | 1.11.0 | TuDoor Attacks |
| CVE-2024-0874 | MEDIUM | 1.11.2 | CD bit response caching issue |

## Impact Summary

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total CVEs eliminated by bumping to v1.14.6 | ~47 dependency + 11 CoreDNS-specific |
| Critical CVEs eliminated | 8 |
| High CVEs eliminated | ~14 |
| Authentication bypass CVEs eliminated | 3 (CVE-2026-33190, CVE-2026-35579, CVE-2026-26017) |

## Remaining Vulnerabilities in v1.14.6

Even after upgrading to v1.14.6, a small number of issues remain. We are
reporting these separately to the CoreDNS PST (security@coredns.io):

| CVE/Advisory | Severity | Package | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| CVE-2026-56852 | HIGH | golang.org/x/text v0.38.0 | Fix in v0.39.0 |
| GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf | HIGH | google.golang.org/grpc v1.82.0 | Fix in v1.82.1 |
| GO-2026-5932 | UNKNOWN | golang.org/x/crypto v0.53.0 | openpgp deprecated |
| CVE-2022-2835 | MEDIUM | CoreDNS | No fix available |
| CVE-2022-2837 | MEDIUM | CoreDNS | No fix available |
| CVE-2023-30464 | MEDIUM | CoreDNS | No fix available |

## Request

1. **Can the Kubernetes release team bump CoreDNS to v1.14.6 (or latest
   compatible) in an upcoming v1.35.x patch release?**
2. Is there a defined process or cadence for CoreDNS version updates
   within Kubernetes patch releases?
3. Until a patch release is available, is manually upgrading CoreDNS
   to v1.14.6 within a Kubernetes v1.35.1 cluster a supported and
   tested configuration?
4. Are there any known compatibility issues between CoreDNS v1.14.6
   and Kubernetes v1.35.1?

## Additional Information
We have confirmed that Kubernetes v1.36.3 (the latest release) also ships CoreDNS v1.13.1
```
[root@kcp1 ~]# kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/kube-scheduler:v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1
registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10.1
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0
```

title: Kubernetes ships etcd 3.6.6-0 with 61 CVEs (2 Critical) across all supported versions — upstream 3.7.1 available
content:
/sig cluster-lifecycle
/sig etcd
/kind bug
/priority critical-urgent

## Summary

All currently supported Kubernetes versions (v1.34.x, v1.35.x, v1.36.x)
ship `registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0`, which contains **61 known
vulnerabilities** in the etcd binary alone including **2 Critical**.
The upstream etcd project has released v3.7.1.

etcd 3.6.6-0 has the **oldest dependencies of any Kubernetes control
plane component**, compiled with Go 1.24.10 and gRPC 1.71.1.

## Confirmed Across All Supported K8s Versions
```
$ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.35.1
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

$ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.35.7
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

$ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0
```

## Scan Results
```
$ trivy image registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

etcd binary: 61 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 32, MEDIUM: 23, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 3)
etcdctl: 42 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 20, MEDIUM: 17, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 2)
etcdutl: 59 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 30, MEDIUM: 23, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 3)
```

## CRITICAL Vulnerabilities

| CVE | Library | Installed | Fixed | Title |
|-----|---------|-----------|-------|-------|
| CVE-2026-33186 | google.golang.org/grpc | **v1.71.1** | 1.79.3 | **gRPC-Go: Authorization bypass due to improper HTTP/2 path validation** |
| CVE-2025-68121 | Go stdlib | **v1.24.10** | 1.24.13 | **Incorrect certificate validation during TLS session resumption** |

**Both are directly exploitable in etcd:**
- etcd IS a gRPC server — gRPC is its primary communication protocol
- etcd uses mTLS for peer-to-peer and client communication

## etcd-Specific CVEs 

etcd 3.6.6 has additional CVEs due to its older Go stdlib (1.24.10):

| CVE | Severity | Title |
|-----|----------|-------|
| CVE-2025-61726 | HIGH | Memory exhaustion in net/url query parameter parsing |
| CVE-2025-61729 | HIGH | DoS via excessive resource consumption in crypto/x509 |
| CVE-2025-61727 | MEDIUM | x509 subdomain constraint doesn't restrict wildcard SANs |
| CVE-2025-61728 | MEDIUM | Excessive CPU in archive/zip |
| CVE-2025-61730 | MEDIUM | TLS handshake messages at incorrect encryption level |
| CVE-2025-47913 | HIGH | SSH client panic (x/crypto 0.36.0 specific) |
| CVE-2025-47914 | MEDIUM | SSH Agent DoS via malformed messages |
| CVE-2025-58181 | MEDIUM | DoS via unbounded GSSAPI memory consumption |
| CVE-2025-47911 | MEDIUM | Quadratic HTML parsing complexity |
| CVE-2025-58190 | MEDIUM | Infinite HTML parsing loop |

## Impact

etcd stores **all Kubernetes cluster state** including secrets,
configmaps, RBAC policies, and service accounts. A compromise of
etcd means complete cluster compromise. The CRITICAL gRPC
authorization bypass (CVE-2026-33186) and TLS certificate
validation failure (CVE-2025-68121) in the component that guards
all cluster data is an urgent concern.

## Request

1. **Bump etcd to 3.7.1** (or latest compatible) in upcoming
   patch releases for v1.35.x and v1.36.x
2. If 3.7.x has compatibility concerns, at minimum bump to a
   newer 3.6.x patch (if one exists with updated dependencies)
3. Is there a tracking issue for etcd version updates?

## How to Reproduce

```bash
trivy image registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

title: [cri-o] `/metrics/cadvisor` missing `namespace`, `pod`, `container` labels when using CRI stats
content:
### What happened?

CRI runtimes provide labels like `id`, `name`, and `image`, but not the Kubernetes-level `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels. The cadvisor path adds these via `containerPrometheusLabelsFunc` in `pkg/kubelet/server/server.go`, but the CRI path has no equivalent.

This means any monitoring setup that queries by `namespace`, `pod`, or `container` on cadvisor metrics (which is most of them) breaks when the feature gate is turned on.

### What did you expect to happen?

`/metrics/cadvisor` should produce the same label set regardless of whether the cadvisor or CRI stats path is active.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate on the kubelet
2. Run a workload
3. Scrape `/metrics/cadvisor`
4. Observe that metrics like `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` are missing `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels

### Anything else we need to know?

Two approaches:

**Option 1: Kubelet resolves labels at scrape time**

Call `ListPodSandbox` and `ListContainers` in the metrics collector to build sandbox/container ID → metadata maps, then append `namespace`, `pod`, `container` to each metric. This follows the same pattern `criStatsProvider.getPodAndContainerMaps` uses for `/stats/summary`. The two RPCs are local gRPC calls and the scrape interval is typically 30s, so the cost is low.

**Option 2: Extend the CRI API**

`ListPodSandboxMetrics` currently returns metrics keyed by sandbox/container ID, but without any pod or container metadata. The runtime already has this metadata, it receives `PodSandboxMetadata` (name, namespace, uid) during `RunPodSandbox` and `ContainerMetadata` (name) during `CreateContainer`, and stores both for the lifetime of the sandbox/container.

Adding these existing metadata fields to `PodSandboxMetrics` and `ContainerMetrics` would let the kubelet read `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` directly from the metrics response without any additional RPCs or cache lookups.

A lighter variant: only add the pod UID to `PodSandboxMetrics`. The kubelet can then look up name and namespace from its internal pod cache (keyed by UID), and resolve container names by matching container IDs against the cached pod status.

/sig node
/kind bug

---

title: maxSurge for node draining or how to meet availability requirements when draining nodes by adding pods
content:
### What would you like to be added?

A way to drain nodes by adding more pods elsewhere to meet PodDisruptionBudgets.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, when there is a Deployment, it can be configured to have a `maxSurge` to avoid going under the amount of replicas the deployment requires while allowing for a new release to be rolled out. This parameter allows adding extra pods before subtracting the old ones so that the "replicas" number required is always met as a minimum,

This feature (to my knowledge) is only available when releasing new versions of an application, however when draining nodes this would be extremely useful.

Usual cluster maintenance is done by adding new nodes before removing old ones. This means all the pods in the node need to be evicted and there is usually space for one more of each of the old node in the new node. Current solutions such as the PodDisruptionBudget or Eviction API are trying to make sure that substracting pods from the current amount don´t break anything, however the possibility of temporarily having one extra pod of each deployment is not contemplated at the moment.

This request is asking for the ability to use a surplus of pods to meet all constraints for safe eviction.

Some side notes to stress the importance. Although when operating evictions on large workloads lack of PDBs or PDBs with minAvailable/maxUnavailable settings work fine. When moving deployments with 1 replicas or HPA controlled deployments that are currently scaled down enough the problem is aggravated and can only be solved through a few inefficient means, which is acerbated if node maintenance is done automatically (such as GKE, and other cloud services)

Just in case, this is a limitation that should only be counted against Deployments with `strategy.type=RollingUpdate`.

Ways to deal with this situation currently:

1. Have a `minReplicas`/`replicas` to `>1`, and a PDB with `maxUnavailable=1` when it's known that the autoscaler if in use, it's usually scaled on the lower end. Pros: There is no downtime, Cons: Waste of resources.
2. Do nothing, and deal with eventual downtimes. Pros: No waste of resources, Cons: There is downtime in the deployment

It's important to understand that any controller (deployment, or any other workload) and disruption are two distinct mechanism having different roles, although their  functionality is complementary when we're talking about ensuring high availability.
I'd like to stress here the high availability factor, which is at the front and center when talking about PDBs. I will admit it's challenging to have any further discussion without that prerequisite fullfilled. 
In a similar vein, when talking about HPAs, there's an option for minimum number of replicas, which ensure the application always maintains the HA pre-reqs. 

Moving on to the subject of configuring a rolling update (in case of a deployment), versus responding to external disruptions (in this case, PDB being an external actor is equal to invoking `kubectl delete` by the user). The reason we have
the ability to have a detailed rollout is coming from the fact that it is a process fully operated by the owning controller. Whereas in all other situations (ie. any external errors or disruptions), the controller's goal is to reach the desired state as quickly as possible. 

Speaking from my own experience, we've had multiple instances of problems when PDBs were blocking the upgrades, due to users setting the allowed replicas down to bare minimum. We solved it by [adding an alert](https://github.com/openshift/cluster-kube-controller-manager-operator/blob/d95b0c25ba55c4ef8e09e56461562ee60b22d51c/manifests/0000_90_kube-controller-manager-operator_05_alerts.yaml#L25-L44) which looks at PDBs and notifies administrators in those cases. Since then we haven't seen any problems, or cluster administrators were aware that problems might popup during upgrade and were able to solve these problems even before initiating the upgrades. 

Having said all of the above, [SIG Apps](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/master/sig-apps) meeting happens on every other Monday, next occurrence is planned for September 18. If you're interested, I'd be happy to hear more about your use cases and the problems you're struggling with. 

Hello Maciej,

I will do my best to join the monday call.

Just for other people reading the thread, my use case are all the
miscellaneous apps that are needed to run some services on top of
kubernetes (such as knative admission controller, external-dns, etc.), as
well as any other app that just doesn't need scaling.

These apps have PDBs that make sure that there is always at least a single
instance running (hence it makes sense that the minimum availability of the
PDB is 1), however running more than one instance at a time would be a
waste of resources.

I understand there is ownership and interactions between the different
controllers, and some of my ideas were revolving around creating a new
attribute, however it was brought to my attention that the `maxSurge` field
perfectly describes the situation, "I'm okay with having up to X instances
for a while".

Regarding the PDB blocking upgrade issue, I had those too, however because
we are running in GKE and nodes get recycled in a regular basis, we can't
have a cluster operator be waiting for a node maintenance to happen (nor we
want to).

I hope I was able to give enough context,

Cheers, Javier

title: K8s v1.35.6 - [CVE-2026-46595] unfixed on AKS 1.35.6 shipping images: azure-cns v1.8.6-0, tigera/operator v1.40.2, calico v3.31.2 (golang.org/x/crypto < 0.52.0)
content:
## Summary

`CVE-2026-46595` (SSH source-address-check bypass in `golang.org/x/crypto`, fixed in `v0.52.0`) is still present in several images that AKS 1.35.6 ships (via the 2026-07-17 release train):

- `mcr.microsoft.com/containernetworking/azure-cns:v1.8.6-0`
- `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/tigera/operator:v1.40.2`
- `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/node:v3.31.2`
- `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/typha:v3.31.2`
- `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/kube-controllers:v3.31.2`

Clusters on `automaticChannel=patch` + `nodeOsUpgradeChannel=NodeImage` receive the current AKS 1.35 shipping set and cannot bypass these tags. The [2026-07-17 release notes](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases/tag/2026-07-17) `Component updates` section does not list azure-cns / tigera-operator / calico bumps, and the earlier [2026-06-19](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases/tag/2026-06-19) release notes are similarly silent, so no in-place refresh has landed yet on the 1.35 track.

## CVE details

- **CVE:** [CVE-2026-46595](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46595)
- **Package:** `golang.org/x/crypto` SSH server side
- **Vulnerable:** `< 0.52.0`
- **Fixed:** `>= 0.52.0`
- **Source of fix:** [golang/go#79570](https://go.dev/issue/79570), CL [781642](https://go.dev/cl/781642), [golang-announce](https://groups.google.com/g/golang-announce/c/a082jnz-LvI)
- **CVSS 3.1 (CISA-ADP):** 10.0 Critical

## Per-image evidence (upstream `go.mod` at the tag AKS ships)

| Image tag on AKS 1.35 | Upstream `go.mod` reference | `golang.org/x/crypto` |
|---|---|---|
| `azure-cns:v1.8.6-0` | [`Azure/azure-container-networking@v1.8.6` go.mod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure/azure-container-networking/v1.8.6/go.mod) | **`v0.46.0`** — vulnerable |
| `tigera/operator:v1.40.2` | [`tigera/operator@v1.40.2` go.mod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tigera/operator/v1.40.2/go.mod) | **`v0.43.0`** — vulnerable |
| `calico/node:v3.31.2` / `typha:v3.31.2` / `kube-controllers:v3.31.2` | [`projectcalico/calico@v3.31.2` go.mod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.2/go.mod) | **`v0.43.0`** — vulnerable |

## Live confirmation (representative AKS 1.35.6 cluster)
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[]}{range .status.containerStatuses[]}{.image}{"|"}{.imageID}{"\n"}{end}{end}'

Returns, among other rows:
mcr.microsoft.com/containernetworking/azure-cns:v1.8.6-0|sha256:7d200184b363d51d2abe9665c60fe8113bbfd6d8708d9aa4806a2d7c55c4e8fa
mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/tigera/operator:v1.40.2|sha256:35f43a5fdc867629b3b8604f7fc8666e2f919778411d86adc6761b18f355e5f3
mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/node:v3.31.2|sha256:5255c2844abb4eea023cd15ceda5380d5bab3d5cf714fd113774597d2265f876
mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/typha:v3.31.2|sha256:f993b68a1d96f7072e0ec5ee6d0d3c9dce8fc37746ad160e262c8c753f6f9eb1
mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/kube-controllers:v3.31.2|sha256:7308b279c79816c9386a593644814a7f0f5caaf3b753982cbf226953782524ee


The `NodeImage` channel weekly rotation only replaces the underlying VM VHD; it does not change the tag pinned by the AKS control plane for these system-addon images. Only a new AKS 1.35.x patch that refreshes these component images can clear the finding.

## Request

Please ship a new AKS 1.35.x patch (and equivalent on any still-supported minor that also uses these tags) that includes:

1. `azure-cns` rebuilt against `golang.org/x/crypto >= 0.52.0` (the `Azure/azure-container-networking` `main` branch already carries a newer minor; a v1.8.x patch or a bump to the newer minor would work).
2. `tigera/operator` and the three `calico/*` images rebuilt against `golang.org/x/crypto >= 0.52.0`. This will most likely arrive when `tigera/operator` and `projectcalico/calico` cut new patches; a re-tag in the `mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/...` mirror is what's ultimately needed on the AKS side.

If work is already in flight, a pointer to the target AKS release date would be very helpful for downstream planning.

## Real-world exploitability

None of these five binaries expose an SSH server that uses non-publickey callbacks, so the practical exploitability of CVE-2026-46595 in these images is effectively nil. The concern here is scanner hygiene / compliance: AKS-managed pods carry a CVSS-10 CVE that consumers cannot patch or override, and no in-place upgrade path currently clears it.

Thanks!

---

### Timeline — grpc-go & Calico upstream

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2026-03-18 | grpc-go **v1.79.3** released with the fix (same day as advisory) |
| 2026-03-21 | CVE published to NVD → **Wiz starts counting Age** |
| 2026-04-15 | Calico v3.31.5 — still bundles grpc v1.72.2 (vulnerable) |
| 2026-05-01 | Calico v3.32.0 — still vulnerable |
| **2026-06-19** | **Calico v3.31.6 released — bumps grpc to v1.79.3 ✅** |
| **2026-06-27** | **Calico v3.32.1 released (latest) — grpc v1.79.3 ✅** |
| 2026-07-28 | **Microsoft AKS mirror still ships calico v3.31.2** — verified via `kubectl` on `us-clink-dev` |

Calico upstream released tag bundling it (v3.31.6, 2026-06-19). Microsoft AKS has **not** yet rebuilt/mirrored the fixed calico tag — that is the current blocker on our clusters.

---

### Upstream go.mod proof (2026-07-28)

| Calico tag | `google.golang.org/grpc` | Status |
|---|---|---|
| [v3.31.2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.2/go.mod) (running) | v1.72.2 | Vulnerable |
| [v3.31.6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.6/go.mod) | **v1.79.3** | Fixed ✅ |
| [v3.32.1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.32.1/go.mod) | **v1.79.3** | Fixed ✅ |

kubectl get pods -A -o json \
  | jq -r '.items[].status.containerStatuses[]?.image' \
  | grep -Ei "calico|tigera" | sort -u

# mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/calico/typha:v3.31.2
# mcr.microsoft.com/mirror/quay/tigera/operator:v1.40.2

title: The crictl test fails on kOps
content:
### Which jobs are failing?

pull-kops-kubernetes-e2e-ubuntu-gce-build

### Which tests are failing?

[sig-node] crictl should be able to run crictl on the node

### Since when has it been failing?

26.08.2025

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/kops-presubmits#pull-kops-kubernetes-e2e-ubuntu-gce-build

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Related to changes added by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133476:
```
exitCode=127 stdout="" stderr="sh: 1: /home/kubernetes/bin/crictl: not found\n", might retry
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The  path for the `crictl` binary has been hardcoded to `/home/kubernetes/bin/crictl`. This is something specific to ContainerOS.
Additionally, `crictl` is not a requirement for a node to run, so maybe this should be a feature-specific test like `[Feature:crictl]`.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig-node

---

/cc @SergeyKanzhelev @mauriciopoppe @ameukam 

/sig node


@hakman do we have to switch these toggles on?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/commit/e8419e29c447650fd5ed0b88b02e8aeaa3229ac0
https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/commit/96a7fd89885f1a3c8df9130206a82066c245e22e

@dims That won't help as the path is hardcoded in the test. Already tried in https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/pull/17605.

In a kOps cluster, is `critctl`'s location added to the `PATH`?

@mauriciopoppe depends on the distro, in most cases the path is `/usr/local/bin/crictl`, but would prefer to not have `crictl` as a fixed dependency for running the test suite. Is there any documentation that marks this a requirement?

The filename is called `crictl.go` so I think it's a dependency. The objective of the test is to verify that running `crictl` remotely through `kubectl exec` is successful across all the nodes in the cluster. 

> Additionally, crictl is not a requirement for a node to run, so maybe this should be a feature-specific test like [Feature:crictl].

I agree, I'll add the feature tag.

Thanks @mauriciopoppe.
Could you also add a few more retries for different paths, or try to run from `PATH`?

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon


/assign @mauriciopoppe 

For the short term I'll revert https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133476. Later, I'll do the refactor once again with a feature tag added.

https://testgrid.k8s.io/kops-gce#kops-gce-latest is green!

@hakman I think we can call it ?

I don’t have any preference here, it can be left open to track the refactor or it can be closed and open another issue to track it.

title: Auto-calculated storage version defaults for alpha to beta transitions
content:
When a resource promotes from alpha to beta, the convention is to immediately use the beta version as the storage version in the same release. Traditionally this has been achieved via manual overrides in [default_storage_factory_builder.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubeapiserver/default_storage_factory_builder.go). [emulatedStorageVersion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/storage/resource_encoding_config.go) was introduced to auto-calculate the storage version and eliminate these overrides, but this introduces a subtle inconsistency. Auto-calculation compares against min-compat version (emulation - 1), so a beta introduced in 1.34 is skipped at emulation 1.34 because min-compat 1.33 doesn't know it, falling back to alpha/non-existent.

This is correct for beta to GA transitions where we want to delay promotion by one release for compatibility, but imo conservative for alpha to beta where the convention is immediate promotion. I think we should default beta to be the storage version the release that they were introduced.

## Triage: `[sig-auth] Projected PodCertificate ... mTLS connection` on capz-master-windows

**TL;DR — this is not a code regression in the PodCertificate feature. The test started running (it was previously *skipped*) because PodCertificateRequest was promoted to GA, which flipped its Ginkgo labels from `[Beta] [Feature:OffByDefault]` to `[Conformance]`. The test itself has a latent problem that manifests as a hard failure on Windows and a flake on Linux.**

### Regression boundary (clean, one build wide)
| | Build | Started | k8s version | mTLS test status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Last **green** | [2079666256385937408](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079666256385937408) | 07-21 20:34Z | `v1.37.0-beta.0.154+a99b1bb8922c1d` | **`skipped`** |
| First **red** | [2079711704756785152](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079711704756785152) | 07-21 23:34Z | `v1.37.0-beta.0.177+60a99a22a57769` | **`failed`** |

The junit test *name* changes across the boundary — proof the skip→run flip is the trigger:
- green: `...establish an mTLS connection [Beta] [Feature:OffByDefault]` → `status="skipped"`
- red: `...establish an mTLS connection [MinimumKubeletVersion:1.37] [Conformance]` → `status="failed"`

### What changed in the window
23 commits (`a99b1bb8922c1d..60a99a22a57769`). The only one touching this feature — and the mechanism — is:

- **`57c6b19abb8` "Promote PodCertificateRequest to GA (v1)" — [PR #139579](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139579)** (merge `c6977342eb5`, merged 07-21 17:17Z, first appears in the 23:34Z build).

GA promotion removes `[Feature:OffByDefault]`/`[Beta]` and adds `[Conformance]`, so the conformance/default suite now executes this test instead of skipping it. **The PR did not break the feature; it exposed a pre-existing test/environment issue by un-skipping the test.**

### Why it fails (mechanism — Windows vs Linux differ)
On the first-red Windows build, the **server pod comes up healthy**:
```
event for server-...: Started: Container started
projected-podcertificate-.../server-... Container server ready: true, restart count 0
```
…but the **client cannot resolve the ClusterIP Service DNS name**:
```
client.go:71] ... Get "https://server.projected-podcertificate-3277.svc/spiffe-echo":
  dial tcp: lookup server.projected-podcertificate-3277.svc: no such host
```
So this is a **Windows service-DNS/networking timing problem**, not a certificate/mTLS problem. The test's `gomega.Eventually` only waits **30s** with the fully-qualified `.svc` name (no trailing `cluster.local`), which is tight for Windows DNS/kube-proxy programming. On **Windows the failure is deterministic (35/35, 100%)**; the same test is only an **intermittent flake on Linux**.

### Blast radius (this is not Windows-only)
The k8s-triage board shows the un-skipped test now failing across many jobs, confirming the promotion — not Windows — is the common cause:
- **Windows, 100% fail:** `ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows`, `-windows-2025`, `-containerd-nightly-windows`, `ci-kubernetes-e2e-windows-containerd-gce-master`, `-win2022-...`
- **Linux/other, intermittent:** `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-{features,enabled,conformance}`, `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce`, `kind-conformance-parallel`, `kops`, `s390x-conformance`, plus presubmits (`pull-kubernetes-conformance-kind-ga-only-parallel`, `pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce`, etc.).

Because it's now `[Conformance]` and flaky on Linux presubmits too, this will intermittently block PR merges.

### Classification
**Real, actionable test/infra defect exposed by a GA promotion — not a regression in PodCertificate runtime code, and not a pure flake** (clear datable onset tied to a specific commit). The e2e test as written is not robust on Windows (service DNS not ready within 30s) and is timing-sensitive on Linux.

### Suggested next steps for sig-auth
1. Loop in the promotion author/reviewers (PR #139579, `@yt2985` / `tinatingyu`) and the test authors.
2. Harden the test before it stays in the conformance gate: increase the `Eventually` timeout (30s → e.g. 2–3m), and/or wait for the Service endpoints/DNS to be resolvable (or gate the mTLS test as `[LinuxOnly]` / add a Windows skip) — `test/e2e/auth/projected_podcertificate.go:105-115`.
3. If a quick fix isn't available, consider temporarily removing `[Conformance]` (or skipping on Windows) to unblock the release-informing board and presubmits.

title: kubectl patch: 'map does not contain declared merge key' error lacks actionable context
content:
## What happened

When using `kubectl patch` with a strategic merge patch on a list field without providing the required merge key, users see the following error:

```
Error from server: map: map[hostPath:map[path:/var/lib/kubelet/pods]] does not contain declared merge key: name
```

## What I expected

The error should explain:
1. **Which field** requires the merge key
2. **What** a merge key is and why it is required
3. **How to fix it** — i.e. include the merge key field in each list item
4. A short example of the correct format

## Reproduction

```bash
# Attempt to patch a container list without providing the "name" merge key
kubectl patch pod mypod --type=strategic -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"image":"nginx:1.25"}]}}'
```

Expected: helpful error explaining that each list item needs `"name": "<container-name>"`
Actual: `map: map[...] does not contain declared merge key: name`

## Root cause

The error originates from `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/mergepatch/errors.go` line 36:

```go
func ErrNoMergeKey(m map[string]interface{}, k string) error {
    return fmt.Errorf("map: %v does not contain declared merge key: %s", m, k)
}
```

The message prints the full map contents (potentially verbose) but provides no guidance on what the user needs to do to fix the patch.

## Suggested improvement

## Triage: `ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows` — AKS retired v1.33.5 from standard support (infra, **not** a k8s regression)

**Verdict: infrastructure / external-dependency breakage.** Azure AKS stopped offering **v1.33.5** on the standard tier (it is now LTS-only). This job creates an **AKS-hosted management cluster** to run CAPZ, and that `az aks create` step now fails before any Windows e2e test runs. Nothing in kubernetes/kubernetes caused this and no k8s code change can fix it.

### Failure signature (the `setup` "test")
```
ERROR: (K8sVersionNotSupported) Managed cluster capz-conf-... is on version 1.33.5,
which is only available for Long-Term Support (LTS). ... use [az aks get-versions] ...
Code: K8sVersionNotSupported
```
This aborts at the **`create resource group and management cluster`** step, so every downstream test is reported as failed setup.

### Regression boundary (job history)
| | Build | Time (UTC) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Last green | [2079666256385937408](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079666256385937408) | 2026-07-21 20:34 | SUCCESS |
| First red (streak) | [2079711704756785152](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079711704756785152) | 2026-07-21 23:34 | FAILURE — *different cause* (cluster came up, timed out later) |
| First `K8sVersionNotSupported` | [2079757215312384000](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079757215312384000) | 2026-07-22 02:35 | FAILURE |
| Reported build | [2079848839686131712](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2079848839686131712) | 2026-07-22 08:39 | FAILURE |
| Latest checked | [2080258677700300800](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows/2080258677700300800) | 2026-07-23 11:48 | FAILURE |

The AKS-version error is **continuous and deterministic from 07-22 02:35 onward** — this is a hard block, not a flake. (Note the very first red at 23:34 on 07-21 was a *different, transient* failure where the mgmt cluster actually provisioned; the AKS retirement kicked in on the next run.)

### Why this is not a k8s code change
`started.json` for both the last-green and the recurring-red builds shows the **identical** `repo-commit`:
```
kubernetes/kubernetes: 18bafa268a916c06b0da44fb78c40b5fac6c6eda   (both green and red)
```
Empty kubernetes commit window ⇒ the cause is outside k8s. The moving parts this job builds/pulls at HEAD are `kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api-provider-azure@main`, `cloud-provider-azure@master`, `windows-testing@master`, plus the **AKS service itself**. The AKS-hosted mgmt cluster's version (1.33.5) is chosen by CAPZ's AKS-mgmt tooling, not by the k8s job config (`config/jobs/kubernetes-sigs/sig-windows/release-master-windows.yaml` pins only `KUBERNETES_VERSION=latest` for the *workload* cluster, nothing about the mgmt-cluster version).

### Where the fix belongs
- **SIG:** this is **sig-windows / CAPZ**, not sig/k8s-infra code. The mgmt-cluster AKS version needs bumping to a currently-supported non-LTS version (`az aks get-versions`), or the creation pinned appropriately. Fix lives in **kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api-provider-azure** (the `aks-mgmt` / `templates/test/ci` bootstrap that sets the AKS management-cluster version) and/or **kubernetes-sigs/windows-testing** scripts — cc @kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api-provider-azure-maintainers.
- Suggested label move: this is `kind/failing-test` but belongs with **sig/windows** (+ CAPZ) rather than sig/k8s-infra; the failure is environmental and will clear once the mgmt AKS version is updated.

**Bottom line for @dims:** Real, non-flaky, but external — AKS deprecated the 1.33.5 management-cluster version out of the standard tier on ~07-22, breaking `az aks create` at setup. No kubernetes/kubernetes commit is implicated (same SHA green→red). Route to sig-windows/CAPZ to bump the AKS management-cluster version; no k8s revert applies.

title: Failure cluster [ea667941...] `Failed to create master instance due to non-retryable error`
content: ### Failure cluster [ea6679417165f10786e6](https://go.k8s.io/triage#ea6679417165f10786e6) ##### Error text: ``` error during ./hack/e2e-internal/e2e-up.sh: exit status 1 ``` #### Recent failures: [7/31/2026, 12:55:11 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-containerd](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-containerd/2083053834405416960) [7/31/2026, 12:49:11 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce/2083052328499286016) [7/31/2026, 12:49:11 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-slow](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-slow/2083052328826441728) [7/31/2026, 12:45:40 AM ci-benchmark-kube-dns-master](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-benchmark-kube-dns-master/2083051318036926464) [7/31/2026, 12:45:10 AM ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-network-proxy-grpc](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-network-proxy-grpc/2083051317680410624) /kind failing-test --- **Root cause.** This was not caused by a change in Kubernetes code. It was a bad image release in the `cos-cloud` GCP project, and Google later rolled it back. What happened: - On 2026-07-31 at 00:14 UTC, Google published a new COS image, `cos-129-19506-299-61`, into the `cos-129-lts` image family. Normally the older image is marked as deprecated at the same time. This time it was not, so the family briefly held two active images, `-60` and `-61`. - `kube-up` looks up the boot image in `cluster/gce/util.sh` with `gcloud compute images list --filter="family:cos-129-lts ..."`. That command returns every active image in the family. It returned both names, joined by a newline. - The two joined names made an invalid `sourceImage` URL. Creating the master VM then failed with `Failed to create master instance due to non-retryable error`. Every GCE e2e job hit this. About 152 builds across 51 jobs failed. - Between about 05:00 and 06:00 UTC, Google rolled the release back. They marked `-61` as deprecated and set `-60` as its replacement. After that, the image lookup returned one name again and the jobs recovered without any change to Kubernetes. E.g. `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-network-proxy-grpc` failed at 00:44, 02:45, and 04:45 UTC, and passed from 06:45 UTC on. To keep this from happening again, the image lookup should take exactly one image. We can add `--sort-by=~creationTimestamp --limit=1` to the two `images list` calls in `cluster/gce/util.sh` (master at line 62, node at line 82), or switch to `gcloud compute images describe-from-family`. /sig cluster-lifecycle testing /triage accepted

These tests are still flaking, but now for a different reason than before.

When the second Pod to bind expectedly fails with "claim got allocated elsewhere", a race starts between the Pod status update to add the `PodScheduled=False` condition and the next binding attempt. The test fails when the next binding attempt succeeds before the `PodScheduled=False` update. In that case, the Pod has been successfully scheduled but the status update for the previous attempt overrides the `PodScheduled=True` condition set when binding succeeded.

@dom4ha Does that sound plausible?

There are a few ways we could fix this:
- Guard the `PodScheduled=False` update on the Pod's `resourceVersion`.
- In the DRA plugin, prevent the "claim got allocated elsewhere" error from failing binding when the expected allocation matches the actual allocation.
- Allocate the ResourceClaim with the PodGroup instead of the first Pod to eliminate contentious status updates in the normal case. There's an [open thread](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5976#discussion_r3327312421) to discuss this on the KEP.
