title: e2e: remove usage of the DeprecatedMightBeMasterNode function from the e2e testing framework
content:
EDIT: the function was renamed to DeprecatedMightBeMasterNode, but the remove action is still pending.

instead of making assumptions that a node is "master" or not, we should make the choices more granular - e.g. can this node host workloads? we should remove usage of the function `IsMasterNode` from `e2e/framework`

see discussion here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/80021#issuecomment-511507244

part of:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/75601

help wanted!

cc @andrewsykim @oomichi @alejandrox1 
/area e2e-test-framework
/sig testing
/kind cleanup


---

/remove-kind feature


cc

I'd be happy to take this. Should `IsMasterNode` be replaced with something?
/assign

> Should IsMasterNode be replaced with something?

that's the tricky part...
there is no sane way in kubernetes to tell if a node hosts a control plane or not.

which means that any calls to IsMasterNode have to be replaced with something that solves the underlying problem - for example are we calling IsMasterNode because we want to know if this node accepts workloads? or are we calling it to determine if there is a controller-manager on the node so that we can scrape metrics from it.


@neolit123 
This issue seems interesting for me, because I am facing a conformance test issue which seems related to this on my local environment.
Even if a node is master, the node can host workload if the taint is removed from the node.
So do we want to use some function which checks a node is tainted instead of current  IsMasterNode()?

Some investigation related to this issue:
Now all 7 callers of `IsMasterNode()` are
```
e2e/framework/metrics/metrics_grabber.go:               if system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) {
e2e/framework/metrics/latencies.go:             if system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) {
e2e/framework/resource_usage_gatherer.go:               if (options.Nodes == MasterNodes) && !system.IsMasterNode(pod.Spec.NodeName) {
e2e/framework/resource_usage_gatherer.go:               if (options.Nodes == MasterAndDNSNodes) && !system.IsMasterNode(pod.Spec.NodeName) && pod.Labels["k8s-app"] != "kube-dns" {
e2e/framework/resource_usage_gatherer.go:               if options.Nodes == AllNodes || system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) || dnsNodes[node.Name] {
e2e/framework/node/resource.go:         if system.IsMasterNode(n.Name) {
e2e/framework/node/wait.go:                     if !system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) {
```
1. `e2e/framework/metrics/metrics_grabber.go:               if system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) {`
**Unnecessary to be changed**
This is for knowing a master node is registered or not for grabbing metrics.
So I think we can keep this code as current one because it is not related to workload.
2. `e2e/framework/metrics/latencies.go:             if system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) {`
**Unnecessary to be changed**
The same as 1
3. `e2e/framework/resource_usage_gatherer.go:               if (options.Nodes == MasterNodes) && !system.IsMasterNode(pod.Spec.NodeName) {`
**Unnecessary to be changed**
The callers of `NewResourceUsageGatherer()` specify the node mode(MasterNodes, MasterAndDNSNodes or AllNodes) and the function uses `IsMasterNode()` for knowing a pod is in the specified node mode.
So current usage seems valid for the function purpose.
4. `e2e/framework/resource_usage_gatherer.go:               if (options.Nodes == MasterAndDNSNodes) && !system.IsMasterNode(pod.Spec.NodeName) && pod.Labels["k8s-app"] != "kube-dns" {`
**Unnecessary to be changed**
The same as 3
5. `e2e/framework/resource_usage_gatherer.go:               if options.Nodes == AllNodes || system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) || dnsNodes[node.Name] {`
**Unnecessary to be changed**
The same as 3
6. `e2e/framework/node/resource.go:         if system.IsMasterNode(n.Name) {`
**Necessary to be changed**
The caller `GetMasterAndWorkerNodes()` returns master nodes and worker nodes as the function name.
However if a master node is not tainted, the master node also can host workload pods.
So here should be changed for matching the usage of `GetMasterAndWorkerNodes()`.
7. `e2e/framework/node/wait.go:                     if !system.IsMasterNode(node.Name) {`
**Necessary to be changed**
The caller `WaitForTotalHealthy()` is waiting for some pods become active.
And the pods are kube-proxy, fluentd-elasticsearch and node-problem-detector.
That means the function expects these pods should run on non-master nodes.
However if a master node is not tainted, the master node also can host these pods.
So we need to change the function.

> Even if a node is master, the node can host workload if the taint is removed from the node.
So do we want to use some function which checks a node is tainted instead of current IsMasterNode()?

in some cases yes.

system.IsMasterNode will be removed and the idea is not have a function in the framework (or k8s as a whole) that makes node-role assumptions based on node names or labels.

but quite frankly it think the usage of the function is bogus and outdated:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d8695d06b7191db56ebbbc0340da263833c9bb6f/pkg/util/system/system_utils.go#L23-L37

e.g. kubeadm control-plane nodes don't have `master` in their names, unless the user name them like so, so this might or might not work for some bootstrappers or user setups, so by removing the function or changing the behavior of some of these tests we might as well break someone or at least change their expected test results...



@neolit123 
> but quite frankly it think the usage of the function is bogus and outdated:

OMG, I never see the internal code of the function.
Yeah I agree with you here. The function seems fake according to the code.
Usually I am naming master node which include "master" but I didn't know the naming way is mandatory on this function..

yeah, the function has to be removed, one way or another.
by making node name assumptions part of the tests may or may not work depending on the user setup.


Here's the KEP (link to e2e specific part) https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1144/files#diff-55982acee19ca4466736d3b3c150218aR160

Hi! Would this issue be suitable for me as first-time contributor?
I will be happy to help with it, came because of "help wanted" label

I think the issue may be to figure out what the correct replacement is. The code changes are probably not hard but knowing what they should be may be interesting and require buy in.

"good first issue" is used on issues that are targeting for first time contributors, "help wanted" has been a little more contentious :sweat_smile: 

Since a49a554211101f594e55e4b7d4574b535249db58 `IsMasterNode()` has been renamed to `DeprecatedMightBeMasterNode()`.
It is better to change the title for finding the problematic function easily.
(I faced it today ;-) )

we have a retitle command :)
/retitle e2e: remove usage of the DeprecatedMightBeMasterNode function from the e2e testing framework


Interesting, it is helpful command for me :-)

title: Autodetect IP family for e2e testing
content:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:

Introduce a mechanism that allows ~~detecting~~ specifying the IP protocol version used in the e2e testing.


**Why is this needed**:

This is a followup on #70248, my understanding is that in order to discriminate between IPv4 or IPv6  we have to use the test labels and this adds complexity to the testing automation and doesn't allow to send this information to the context of the tests.

Having a mechanism to ~~detect~~ specify the IP protocol will simplify the testing for IPv4 and IPv6 and will allow reusing most of the code.



---

/sig testing
/cc @neolit123 @fabriziopandini @BenTheElder 
/assign @aojea 

Does this make sense?
If affirmative, what should be the best way to add this functionality? 
Checking the code I think that `e2e/framework/test_context.go` or `test/e2e/framework/framework.go` can provide this, don't know if checking some of the cluster config parameters, 🤔 ...


the testing-commons group (sig-testing) maintains the framework, but ideally the decision on how to proceed in terms of adding ipv6 detection should come from sig-network.

possibly having this as agenda for a sig-network meeting is a good start, then discussing it in a testing-commons meeting.

/sig network

> Having a mechanism to detect the IP protocol will simplify the testing for IPv4 and IPv6 and will allow reusing most of the code.

the linked issue is a big one, so i don't have all the context here. but IMO existing tests should just work for ipv6 without the requirement for a new "IPV6" tag in test names.

dual-stack or protocol specific tests should have their descriptions contain the details properly (i.e. what is this test doing)

we might want to add an utility function under:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/framework/networking_utils.go
(there is a PR to move it BTW https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/77377/files)

then such an utility might be useful *only* to tests that need to detect the protocol.

one of the goals is to refactor the code in test_context / framework, so adding this logic there is less preferred.




/area e2e-test-framework

@neolit123 I think that we can add an option to test_context to specify the cluster IP family the same way that exists one for the cloud provider

```
	// Provider identifies the infrastructure provider (gce, gke, aws)
	Provider string

	// The IP Family of the cluster
	IpFamily string
```

this is simpler because when setting up the CI jobs you will know beforehand what IP family you want to test, it also will allow reusing all the e2e code for IPv6 and Dual Stack (cc: @khenidak) and by default will be IPv4, so it´s backward compatible.


Being able to override and specify exactly what you want the test to beleive about your cluster is nice, but ideally it should generally work without specifying _more_ flags. Surely we can detect this?

I was thinking during some time about this,  detecting the IP family is very simple having IPv4 or IPv6 only clusters, but with the introduction of dual stack I´m afraid about the supportability and reliability of the autodetecting mechanisms in the long term. If you see the dual stack PRs there are still a lot of unknowns about the cluster behavior.
My point is, let´s have something first stable that works and is simple, and once dual stack is implemented, we can replace the flag with a function in the framework .

I guess that migrating from a flag variable to a function is straight forward, 

```
// LoopbackIP returns a loopback IP depending on the IP family of the cluster
func LoopbackIP() string {
	switch TestContext.IpFamily {
	case "ipv6":
		return "::1"
	default:
		return "127.0.0.1"	}
}
```

is just replacing `TestContext.IpFamily` by `e2enet.IpFamily`, what do you think?

> is just replacing TestContext.IpFamily by e2enet.IpFamily, what do you think?

in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/80398
`IpFamily` is added as part of the context.

do you mean adding `e2enet.IpFamily()` as a function which will auto-detecting the ip family.
less flags for the framework binary is preferred.


once we have this I will open a new issue to start cleaning up `[Feature:Networking-IPv6]` and `[Feature:Networking-IPv4]` , we no longer need to discriminate based on tags

title: Properly support Unstructured in API Machinery stack
content:
CRDs are implemented by reusing standard API stack and represented as Unstructured. But Unstructured is not properly supported by the stack and there are lots of hacks. This is the umbrella issue for fixing those hacks:

- [x] Properly handling __internal version for Unstructured
- [ ] Add test coverage for Unstructured 
  - to versioning codecs
  - to the conversion stack
  - to the schema
- [x] Remove all hacks from Schema and fail hard on Unstructured
  - currently conversions ignored Unstructured. But the schema code should not try to do the wrong thing for Unstructured, but instead uncovers plumbing errors early.

This should block any further work on conversion.

title: [PodSecurityPolicy] API changes
content:
This is a cover bug to aggregate non-backwards compatible API changes for consideration to the PodSecurityPolicy (i.e. for `v1beta2`).

- [ ] The empty policy should be equivalent to a fully privileged policy. This is a required property of new fields for backwards compatibility, and making all fields behave this way will make the API more consistent. The simplest approach is to default fields to the most permissive value (e.g. `privileged=true`, `allowedCapabilities=*`, etc.). This requires that most fields change to pointer values.

- [ ] All fields should be optional (with the exception of fields with dependencies on other fields, e.g. user MustRunAs), with defaults as described above. The motivation is the same as above, and reduces boilerplate (e.g. for unused features).

- [ ] Organize volume controls. E.g. `AllowedHostPaths`, and [`AllowedFlexVolumes`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53179). As more controls are added for individual volume types, it would be good to have some more structure to these options.

Open for discussion.

---

CC @adelton @pweil- @liggitt 

@kubernetes/sig-auth-proposals 

Security usability issue: RunAsUser and RunAsGroup are disingenuous as alone they allow pod processes to escalate to any user or group (including root) using SUID/SGID. I don't think this is obvious behavior to users of PodSecurityPolicy. Can we modify defaults to disallow this unless explicitly requested?

I found that some types were named inconsistently:
```console
$ grep '^type [^ ]\+ string' pkg/apis/extensions/types.go
type DeploymentStrategyType string
type DeploymentConditionType string
type DaemonSetUpdateStrategyType string
type DaemonSetConditionType string
type ReplicaSetConditionType string
type FSType string
type SELinuxStrategy string
type RunAsUserStrategy string
type FSGroupStrategyType string
type SupplementalGroupsStrategyType string
```
Why `SELinuxStrategy` and `RunAsUserStrategy` don't have `Type` suffix? If it's OK, then why `FSGroupStrategyType` and `SupplementalGroupsStrategyType` have this suffix?

> Why SELinuxStrategy and RunAsUserStrategy don't have Type suffix? If it's OK, then why FSGroupStrategyType and SupplementalGroupsStrategyType have this suffix?

Less a question of why (let's blame me for that one) and more a question of which one to standardize on.  I'd vote for the non-type suffix as it just seems redundant.  

> Less a question of why (let's blame me for that one) and more a question of which one to standardize on.

Yes, indeed, it's not so interesting of why because it's already there. My question was -- how it should be named and how to proceed to that? I posted it here, as removal of the old constants looks like a breaking change. On another hand, it should be possible to introduce the new types without breaking anything.

> I'd vote for the non-type suffix as it just seems redundant.

First I also thought that the suffixes should be removed, but when I did a grep and saw that Deployments/ReplicaSet have such suffixes I started to doubt.

Another proposed breaking change is to change the default behavior for sysctls -- right now `nil` means "allow all":
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a0844c17bfb964e3d1709784203e8404f790116c/pkg/security/podsecuritypolicy/sysctl/mustmatchpatterns.go#L39-L48
I'd suggest to make it stricter by default.

Perhaps, we even can do that change without waiting for major release because sysctl support in Alpha state. WDYT?

CC @sttts 



> Another proposed breaking change is to change the default behavior for sysctls

Hmm, so I stated in the description that I think all fields should default to "allow all". I could maybe be convinced that the default could only allow up to the pod default (e.g. capabilities default to allowing the default set of capabilities, as opposed to allowing all capabilities). I'm worried that this would cause problems if defaults change across API versions of Pods though.

We only allow sysctls that are "safe", which mainly means that pod isolation is good enough to avoid harm using them. But I don't have a strong opinion about the default in PSPs either.

> The empty policy should be equivalent to a fully privileged policy. This is a required property of new fields for backwards compatibility

That only works if all new fields added to the Pod API are restrictive, which will likely not be the case (c.f. https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/1934)

> I stated in the description that I think all fields should default to "allow all". I could maybe be convinced that the default could only allow up to the pod default

That is closer to being workable (assuming new fields in the Pod API default to their current behavior), but is harder to explain

> That is closer to being workable (assuming new fields in the Pod API default to their current behavior), but is harder to explain

Come to think of it, that's more or less what we're doing already:

a new field added to Pods that expands powers (e.g. `rawProc`):
* defaults to whatever value maintains the current behavior / level of power
* the corresponding control field in PSP defaults to preventing the power expansion (otherwise existing PSPs suddenly allow more powerful pods)

a new field added to Pods that allows limiting powers (e.g. `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`):
* defaults to whatever value maintains the current behavior / level of power
* the corresponding control field in PSP defaults to not requiring/setting the limitation (otherwise existing PSPs suddently become more restrictive)

title: Introduce critical performance tests as (manually unblockable) post-submit blockers
content:
As discussed in the release burndown meeting yesterday, here's a briefing of the issue: Most of the folks (@smarterclayton, @liggitt, @jdumars, @gmarek and many from the release team) almost unanimously agreed with the requirement of post-submit blockers. Their absence is affecting us in multiple ways: 1.Release quality: We are shipping the release with a known performance regression violating our SLO (#51899) documented as a [known issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/58315cc33c51f8f4d05364d80f0b66f5d980bad7/release-1.8/release-notes-draft.md#known-issues) - which would potentially leave some users unwilling to upgrade to 1.8. A proper fix to it was infeasible that close to the release, which wouldn't have been the case if we early-blocked on it. OTOH reverting the concerned PR would've also compromised us on release signal and kicked out a correctness fix from the release. 2.Eng productivity: We've spent multiple weeks of eng time to debug/fix the issues involved, complicated further by the fact that multiple of them got piled up due to lack of post blockers: - 2w of my time for running 2 rounds of bisection, debugging/fixing/studying code/logs (3 regressions - #52107 (node OOMs), #51899 (audit-log performance), #51899(kubelet-gc thundering herd)) - 3-4d of @liggitt (senior member from RedHat) examining the issue, going through a PR diff storm, plotting some graphs, etc - 2w of folks from concerned SIGs combined (scalability, api-machinery, node, instrumentation) - involves debugging / PR fixes & reviews / issue reporting - 1w of release team's time combined (long burndown meeting(s) with multiple folks, slack discussions, triaging/understanding/documenting the regressions) 3.Release schedule: The release had to be pushed off by a day to resolve the issue and led to some chaos and discussion few hours before the release ETA. Note that the proposal is not to block until the post-submit is fixed, but to block until we have a clear enough idea about the cause. We should then be able to unblock the queue (possibly manually) and work on the fix independently without needing to block further. This release is a clear example of how a little investment early on can reap huge benefits later. cc @kubernetes/sig-release-members @kubernetes/sig-testing-feature-requests @dims @spiffxp --- Any thoughts/comments that you might have are more than welcome. @jdumars It would be great if you could link to this issue from the release retrospective doc (if there's one). @krzyzacy Assigning it to you, as in you we trust :) Feel free to redirect as apt. Note that this is quite important. cc: @stevekuznetsov @spxtr @cjwagner This will be making an appearance in the retro for sure. @shyamjvs Is this around the same idea as https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/4445? a few ideas: - we had the idea which block the submit queue base on an issue - if the test is fast enough, we can run it as a postsubmit job, and which will provide clear signal for you to catch regressions How about join our sig-testing meeting next Tue and we can talk about it? That one is different.. It's quite a fast one which we can potentially afford to run as a pre-submit and should help us catch few regressions. However our releases are blocked on 5k-node job which often exposes issues that come up only at such scale (for e.g the ones we saw this release). > we had the idea which block the submit queue base on an issue That sounds reasonable, though I assume the workflow is going to be sth like: (test failed) -> (issue created and potentially triaged) -> (SQ blocked on that issue, so it gets people's traction) -> (after looking into it, the submit-queue could be manually unblocked or kept blocked (if required) based on the build-cop's discretion) > How about join our sig-testing meeting next Tue and we can talk about it? Will try to dial in, can't commit at the moment though. @shyamjvs or we have daily community standups if you cannot make the weekly sig-testing meeting SG - Will join on one of the days (mon or tue) next week. Thanks. We may want to consider that prior to code freeze all signal needs to be good, and that it's on the affected sigs to focus before code freeze that any of the long pole post-submits are green. No one felt the pain of the post-submit until it was very late, which was too late. On Fri, Sep 29, 2017 at 3:01 PM, Shyam JVS wrote: > SG - Will join on one of the days (mon or tue) next week. Thanks. > > — > You are receiving this because you were mentioned. > Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub > , > or mute the thread > > . > I know that testgrid is supposed to have notifications, maybe we could start spamming slack and/or email on poor results from a set of jobs until people take notice? [Here](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/tree/master/testgrid/config#email-alerts) is an explanation of how you can enable testgrid email alerts. @kargakis @cjwagner The issue here is not about getting alerts/notifications - we usually know when the tests start failing, especially because they're part of release-blocking suite. The real problem arises due to not blocking on those failures - as that allows for multiple regressions piling up on top of each other making debugging a nightmare, especially for such long-running tests (like we saw this release with 3 regressions, one on top of the other). It would've been much easier and productive to block on the failure and someone taking a quick look to identify the cause and unblock the queue immediately (without even needing to wait till the next run or the fix). I am not against blocking on postsubmits but we need community buy-in. Bring it up in the sig-testing call tomorrow? > It would've been much easier and productive to block on the failure @shyamjvs I believe in the past the benefit of blocking for N people that can actively work on fixing something was strongly outweighed by the detriment of blocking the queue for N*M others that were not affected by the issue, not able to fix it, etc. @smarterclayton can probably expand on that more. It seems like the entire k8s dev community needs to be on board for such a large change. Discussion in sig-testing sounds good. Let's talk about this further tomorrow. @stevekuznetsov - to be fair, k8s dev community was NOT on board with disabling post submit tests. We literally said that if we do that the thing that happened in 1.8 will happen for reasons already posted by @shyamjvs. The question we need to answer is are we really willing to pay with system reliability for the *perceived* slowdown of development - no one is preventing anyone from working on fixed when merge queue is blocked. This is exactly what happens during the "code freeze", and it doesn't slow down the influx of fixes. It slows down the influx of new stuff that's not a fix if anything, but the question is whether it's a bad thing given the state of things. It's not OK if some small group of people (this time it was mostly @shyamjvs and @liggitt if I'm not mistaken) pay the price for that, and spend weeks looking at logs and running experiments. IMO that's very far from a healthy environment. Putting the milestone approval label on because this is pretty important. Can we reach a reasonable consensus on this issue soon? It is affecting our release process/quality. @wojtek-t - fyi hummm cc @cjwagner tide can block merge upon a certain issue right? If that's the case we just need to wait for enabling tide on the main repo. We can try on test-infra. @krzyzacy I don't think that functionality has been implemented yet. @krzyzacy @cjwagner What's the plan of action here? Auto-filing an issue on failure and blocking SQ against it sounds like a good option. In any case, we need some mechanism to block on the failure (and it should be manually overridable). From technical point of view, maybe make tide block on some certain labels, and we can auto or manually apply the label. But we probably need to be obvious to tell people why merge is blocked. @cjwagner WDYT Looking at the times posted in @shyamjvs's summary, I would like to know how blocking the submit queue would have shortened those times. I have concerns that blocking the queue for durations of that length would have severely hampered our productivity and caused us to push the release out for much longer than a day. I would prefer to see a policy of treating the release-*-blocking jobs as blockers to going through gates in the release process (e.g.: entering code freeze, cutting bits, exiting code freeze). If we cannot go through these gates in time, I would prefer to see the entire schedule shifted out by the delay, rather than treating the entirety of the remaining schedule as buffer to be eaten into. @krzyzacy That plan sounds good to me. As discussed in a meeting, if we block by using a special label on issues, people can tell why the merge is blocked by searching github for open issues with that label just as Tide does. We can put links to that query in important places. > I would like to know how blocking the submit queue would have shortened those times. Blocking the SQ would've helped us in at least the following ways: - we accumulated multiple regressions one on top of the other (listed in the PR description). This made debugging time much longer (and unpredictable) than what it would've been if we identified each of them on time. This brings me to the 2nd point.. - not blocking the SQ didn't put enough pressure on the issue for folks to start looking into it, until it was quite late (like @smarterclayton also said in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/53255#issuecomment-333210985) > I have concerns that blocking the queue for durations of that length would have severely hampered our productivity and caused us to push the release out for much longer than a day. I'm not sure if that would've hampered the productivity severely. As I mentioned earlier, the block wouldn't be until the fix is rolled out and we have a green run, it would only be until someone (or a group of folks) look into what caused it (by taking a quick glance at the commit diff, or the logs, or if really really needed a handful of hours of bisection (but this probably can happen with the queue unblocked)). The key need here is to get traction on the issue ASAP, which only post-submit blockers can truly do imo :) I think a little investment early on can save lots of effort later on, as we saw in this release. By not having the blocker, we're essentially postponing solving the problem to a later point - by when it can get more complicated, more time to debug and more human effort involved (especially with performance regressions which can come from pretty much everywhere in the system). I would agree with the "little investment now can save lots of effort later" - that's been shown to be the case for many of these performance issues. Even without blocking the queue, the desired outcome is ensuring that early investment happens. If there is opposition to blocking the queue, are there suggestions on how to best incentivize the rapid triage in event of failure? On Tue, Oct 17, 2017 at 9:07 PM, Shyam JVS wrote: > I would like to know how blocking the submit queue would have shortened > those times. > > Blocking the SQ would've helped us in at least the following ways: > > - we accumulated multiple regressions one on top of the other (listed > in the PR description). This made debugging time much longer (and > unpredictable) than what it would've been if we identified each of them on > time. This brings me to the 2nd point.. > - not blocking the SQ didn't put enough pressure on the issue for > folks to start looking into it, until it was quite late (like > @smarterclayton also said in #53255 > (comment) > > ) > > I have concerns that blocking the queue for durations of that length would > have severely hampered our productivity and caused us to push the release > out for much longer than a day. > > I'm not sure if that would've hampered the productivity severely. As I > mentioned earlier, the block wouldn't be until the fix is rolled out and we > have a green run, it would only be until someone (or a group of folks) look > into what caused it (by taking a quick glance at the commit diff, or the > logs, or if really really needed a handful of hours of bisection (but this > probably can happen with the queue unblocked)). The key need here is to get > traction on the issue ASAP, which only post-submit blockers can truly do > imo :) > > If we cannot go through these gates in time, I would prefer to see the > entire schedule shifted out by the delay, rather than treating the entirety > of the remaining schedule as buffer to be eaten into. > > I think a little investment early on can save lots of effort later on, as > we saw in this release. By not having the blocker, we're essentially > postponing solving the problem to a later point - by when it can get more > complicated, more time to debug and more human effort involved (especially > with performance regressions which can come from pretty much everywhere in > the system). > > — > You are receiving this because you were mentioned. > Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub > , > or mute the thread > > . > If we make sure that tests actually stay green, we can use alerts to notify people when tests go from green to red, or from flaky to consistently failing. SIG Testing has been working on e-mail based alerts from testgrid that would support this. Part of what allows failures to sneak by is when they're red "but passing if you look at the logs." https://k8s-testgrid.appspot.com/release-master-blocking#gce-scale-performance&width=20 This does not seem like a very good candidate to block the release. It's passed once in the past 2 months. https://k8s-testgrid.appspot.com/release-master-blocking#gce-scale-correctness&width=20 This has never passed. title: CRI: seccomp format is changed from docker 1.12 to 1.13.
content:
Ref https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/27978.

1) We are currently relying on docker seccomp profile format;
2) We are supporing docker 1.11-1.13.

As CRI runtime, which format should we follow? Or should we support both?

@yujuhong @feiskyer @mrunalp @mikebrow @timstclair 
/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs @kubernetes/sig-node-api-reviews 

---

The original profile format https://raw.githubusercontent.com/docker/docker/v1.12.3/profiles/seccomp/default.json is old libcontainerd format https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/blob/5274430fee9bc930598cfd9c9dbd33213f79f96e/libcontainer/configs/config.go#L32.

The new profile format https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/profiles/seccomp/default.json is OCI runtime-spec format https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec/blob/master/specs-go/config.go#L558,

Given so, I think CRI should use OCI format, too. And we may want to explicitly define this in CRI that the profile is json marshal of OCI runtime spec.

This is a tricky question.  CRI only has a path to the profile. The path is a string.  The json file itself needs to be in the format supported by the runtime that is parsing the profile.  If CRI wants to pick a winner here, I would suggest picking the OCI runtime spec v1.0 that is used by runc.


@mikebrow Makes sense. Yeah, maybe as long as the profile is supported by the container runtime, it will be fine, and we don't need to enforce any format here.

The problem is that we also have plan to define the default list in Kubernetes, given the current CRI, kubelet will need to generate a profile for the runtime with the default seccomp list. If so, we still need to enforce a format, so that kubelet knows how to generate the profile.

Another option is to define seccomp structure in CRI, but it means that all existing runtimes need to change.

For reference: the bug pointed to above on moby:
```
invalid header field value "oci runtime error: container_linux.go:247: starting container process caused \"empty string is not a valid syscall\"\n"
```
Will have occurred because one of the differences between the two formats is the option for having a single name: string for a syscall was removed leaving only names: []string for a list of sys calls. Thus resulting in an error, after unmarshalling, that there is no valid name for the sys call to go with the sys call action. Old format:
```
{
     "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW",
     "syscalls": [
         {
             "name": "chmod",
             "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO"
         }
     ]
}
```
New format:
```
{
     "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW",
     "syscalls": [
         {
             "names": ["chmod"],
             "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO"
         }
     ]
}
```

Hmm.. well the default seccomp list should only be determined after caps are set, and also after you know what golang runtime.GOARCH you are running the container on. Otherwise you run the risk of having your seccomp list filtering out commands that should otherwise be enabled.  Additionally, certain commands need arguments to be set based on platform.

I put that new default generator over in containerd/containerd... but maybe the best place for it is over in opencontainers runtime spec. Either way we could bring this code over. See https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/master/contrib/seccomp/seccomp_default.go


> Another option is to define seccomp structure in CRI, but it means that all existing runtimes need to change.

This leaves some extra burden to the maintenance of runtimes I think ... especially when the spec needs some change. (also, kind of divert from "standard" ...)

Use oci spec SGTM, and I also +1 mike's idea if we can move `seccomp_default.go` to oci spec.

At least, we may require runtime respect the oci spec and https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/master/contrib/seccomp/seccomp_default.go. Seems we can work out a library to handle this.

Note that this may introduce problems for non OCI compatible runtimes (if any, or potential ones).

+1 for defining kubernetes own profile format, e.g. same with oci spec. This should be defined in both kubernetes API and CRI.

@Random-Liu  For the current problem, we should at least address it in v1.8 release notes.

Gotta love when APIs change out from under you :)

To echo what everyone else has already said:

Until we define any Kubernetes profiles, I think it's OK to leave the profile format up to the runtime (especially since seccomp is still in alpha).

Once we add a Kubernetes default profile(s), or when we push seccomp to beta, we should settle on the OCI spec, which seems like the clear path forward.

Closely related: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/39128

EDIT: Actually, that's basically a dupe.

Moby seems to be parsing seccomp here - https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/profiles/seccomp/seccomp.go

NM I see it is latest build The `wrapped_wrapped_..._kube-dns-config.deleting...` files are all under `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/5586a4ec-8dd8-11e7-9f87-64510658e388/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap`. From offline discussion with @msau42, it could be that if you had "kube-dns-config.deleting" files from a previous version that were not cleaned up, it could overwhelm kubelet. The HEAD kubelet shouldn't be creating new "kube-dns-config.deleting" files. We could add code in kubelet to ignore those directories, but we shouldn't have run into this scenario in production. The bug only happens if you build K8s < 1.7 with go 1.8, which isn't officially supported. Thanks Janet! That confirms my theory of what happened: 1. Local K8s cluster < 1.7 built with go 1.8 hit bug #43534, which created tens of thousands of directories. 2. The kubelet volume directories were leftover when the cluster was brought down. 3. Local K8s cluster on HEAD was brought up. 4. After 3 minutes, the volume reconstruction loop runs, and finds all the leftover directories from 1). 5. It triggers Unmount for each of the thousands of directories, which spawns a go routine per directory. 6. All the go routines exhausts the process limit of 10k threads and the go runtime crashes the process. So we shouldn't hit this issue in production because in step 1), building K8s < 1.7 with go1.8 is [not qualified](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/development.md#go). I also thought about a production scenario where you could have tens of thousands of mounts on a single node, kubelet restarts, and the volume reconstruction triggers operations on each the volumes again. But, according to our [scaling limits documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/cluster-large/), we only allow a max of 100 Pods per node. So to have tens of thousands of mounts on a node means that each Pod uses hundreds of volumes, which I think is unlikely. So based on this, I don't think this is an issue we need to fix right now. We could revisit this again if our max pods/node limit increases significantly. /priority important-longterm [MILESTONENOTIFIER] Milestone Labels **Incomplete** @janetkuo @msau42 **Action required**: This issue requires label changes. title: Ensure that host disk space used by Docker volume is accounted for
content:
From [Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/engine/admin/volumes/volumes/#start-a-container-with-a-volume): > If you start a container with a volume that does not yet exist, Docker creates the volume for you. The following example mounts the volume myvol2 into /app/ in the container. > > ``` > $ docker run -d \ > -it \ > --name devtest \ > -v myvol2:/app \ > nginx:latest > ``` > > Use docker inspect devtest to verify that the volume was created and mounted correctly. Look for the Mounts section: > > ``` > "Mounts": [ > { > "Type": "volume", > "Name": "myvol2", > "Source": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol2/_data", > "Destination": "/app", > "Driver": "local", > "Mode": "", > "RW": true, > "Propagation": "" > } > ], > ``` > > This shows that the mount is a volume, it shows the correct source and destination, and that the mount is read-write. If the docker volume is not backed by a docker volume driver then docker creates a directory on the host machine to back the volume. Kubernetes is implementing a mechanism to control the amount of host disk space a container can use. See the `Local Ephemeral Storage Resource Management` design in https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/991. Purpose of this bug is to make sure that Kubernetes accounts for docker volumes backed by host disk as part of `ephemeral-storage`. /assign @jingxu97 CC @Random-Liu @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs --- @saad-ali This is not a regression. Do we want this be a 1.8 issue? > @saad-ali This is not a regression. Do we want this be a 1.8 issue? +1. Doesn't seem like a 1.8 issue. My understanding is that the `ephemeral-storage` limit is being introduced in 1.8? @jingxu97? Also ref https://github.com/kubernetes-incubator/cri-containerd/issues/186#issuecomment-327390240. ### Background We don't use docker volume in Kubernetes. However, Dockerfile does support [`VOLUME` ](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/#volume), user could create `VOLUME` and write data into it in the Dockerfile. When docker runs the container, it will: 1) create a host volume; 2) copy data from image into the volume; 3) bind mount the volume back to the image. I believe there are users relying on this behavior, at least, `mongo:latest` and [the microservices demo](https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo/blob/master/deploy/kubernetes/complete-demo.yaml) do reply on the `VOLUME`. Actually, not only Docker image. `Volumes` is also supported in [OCI image spec 1.0](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/d9ffa2f05d4dbe917edfdffcafaf427287a26d1c/config.md#properties). It means that all OCI runtimes also need to support it. ### Problem Today kubelet is not aware of these host volumes, and not doing accounting for it. It means that application could arbitrarily use host disk and not being monitored. ### Possible solutions * Option 1: Tell all OCI runtimes to use rootfs directly instead of creating host volumes. * Cons: * Volumes will also be readonly on readonly rootfs (regression), at least [the microservices demo](https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo/blob/master/deploy/kubernetes/complete-demo.yaml) does rely on it; * Performance regression (overlay filesystem copy-up). * Option 2: Change CRI to let runtime return host volumes for containers. * Cons: Need to figure out whether this aligns with our overall design of `Volumes` in Kubernetes. * Option 3: Let container runtime return OCI image config, and let Kubelet do the volume mount. * Cons: * Making assumption on image format. * If we want to support copying data from container rootfs to volume, kubelet needs access to container rootfs, which is tricky; * More burden on kubelet * Option 4: Update pod spec based on image config in admission controller. * Cons: * Making assumption on image format. * Even more tricky; * Option 5: Advertise user not to use it, and use Kubenetes volumes instead. * Cons: * Takes time. * Not user friendly, because they are using it (need to figure out how many users are using it). **Feel like that option 2 is a better near-term solution, and option 4/5 might be a better long-term solution.** /cc @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs Hostpath volumes are not supported because of the inability to identify sharing patterns. Docker volumes described in this context is hostpath volumes to me. @jingxu97 correct me if I got it wrong. > Hostpath volumes are not supported because of the inability to identify sharing patterns. Docker volumes described in this context is hostpath volumes to me. @jingxu97 correct me if I got it wrong. k8s doesn't allow sharing of this types of volumes -- it doesn't pass `-v` when creating a container. This means that so far these volumes are just private, per-container volumes created by docker and will be destroyed along with the container. This is similar to the emptyDir volumes in kubernetes. It's not that useful unless we explicitly support docker volumes. The volume section in the OCI image spec is very vague. It seems like this should be the user's choice to decide what kind of volumes to create for the container instance at run time. I like Option 4 but it seems less viable at this moment. How about a variant of Option 3? After pulling down the image, kubelet can inspect the image to discover these "volumes". It can then create emptyDir or host volumes based on the default policy or pod spec. Next, it can pass these "special mounts" to the runtime via CRI and runtime would be responsible for copying the data if necessary. We still have the problem of recording the volumes and surfacing them properly. > I like Option 4 but it seems less viable at this moment. How about a variant of Option 3? After pulling down the image, kubelet can inspect the image to discover these "volumes". It can then create emptyDir or host volumes based on the default policy or pod spec. Next, it can pass these "special mounts" to the runtime via CRI and runtime would be responsible for copying the data if necessary. We still have the problem of recording the volumes and surfacing them properly. I also prefer letting kubelet make the decision, so that user could define what the underlying storage should be used for the image defined volumes. By default we could use `EmptyDir`, and could define policy for image defined volumes (need api change). For other runtime or image formats which don't care about this, they could just return empty list. > My understanding is that the ephemeral-storage limit is being introduced in 1.8? @jingxu97? Is this feature alpha or beta in 1.8? I think it's ok not to account these volumes for an alpha feature even if we do decide to do so. I'd suggest punting this to the next release or later given that the volumes are not well-supported in kubernetes. >> My understanding is that the ephemeral-storage limit is being introduced in 1.8? @jingxu97? > > Is this feature alpha or beta in 1.8? I think it's ok not to account these volumes for an alpha feature even if we do decide to do so. > I'd suggest punting this to the next release or later given that the volumes are not well-supported in kubernetes. It is alpha so I'm ok with that. Removing from 1.8 milestone. hostpath is by definition is persistent volume which has different lifecyle of pod. The docker volumes also exist outside the lifecycle of a given container, so I think they are like hostpath volumes. For our current local ephemeral storage isolation feature, we do not management hostpath persistent volumes. For persistent volume, we suggest to use new feature of local volume which is normally set up on a separate partition for easy management. If user choose the share local volume on root file system, we cannot manage the use of the local volumes at least for now. > The docker volumes also exist outside the lifecycle of a given container, so I think they are like hostpath volumes. For our current local ephemeral storage isolation feature, we do not management hostpath persistent volumes. Today we practically treat them as private volumes of the container -- there is no sharing and the volume gets removed along with the container. As mentioned https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/52032#issuecomment-327618068, there is no way for pods/containers to share these volumes using kubernetes API. Whether we want to support these volumes and how to support them is a separate question. > hostpath is by definition is persistent volume which has different lifecyle of pod. The docker volumes also exist outside the lifecycle of a given container, so I think they are like hostpath volumes. That is not the case for image specified volumes. For image specified volume, docker creates it when creating the container, and deletes it when deleting the container (Kubelet chooses to do that specifying [`RemoveVolumes`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockershim/docker_container.go#L273)) So I believe the image volumes are still in the scope of `Local Ephemeral Storage Resource Management`. However, we could not manage it before we change CRI and kubelet, so I don't think we could fix this in 1.8. However, we may want to revisit this in 1.9. fwiw, this has been a discussion for us recently. for clusters where we needed to control this, we can optionally run the following: https://github.com/projectatomic/docker-novolume-plugin but its aggressive in that it denies the ability to start a container that uses an image volume. for cri-o, we want the runtime to support "ignore" image volumes, which i think is the right long term behavior for kubernetes. https://github.com/kubernetes-incubator/cri-o/blob/66d96e77e33bf773781e2a8313e8a73b9c679caa/docs/crio.8.md#global-options see --image-volumes parameter for configuring cri-o daemon. fyi @mrunalp @sjenning > for cri-o, we want the runtime to support "ignore" image volumes, which i think is the right long term behavior for kubernetes. @derekwaynecarr The problem is that there are images relying on the image volume, e.g.: 1) Some assumes that image volume should be writable even if rootfs is read-only; 2) Some assumes that their data baked in the image should be copied to the volume mounted. I don't know how many are there, but at least the `mysql` and `mongo` image does use it, and the sock shop demo is relying on these behaviors. https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo Given so, we may still need to support this unless we could tell user not to use this. On the other hand, image volume is part of OCI image spec now, we may want to properly support it. @yujuhong 's comment https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/52032#issuecomment-327618068 sounds like a good option to me. title: CRI: Should kubelet or runtime handle Capability ALL?
content:
`"all"` is not a valid capability string, but docker supports it, e.g. `docker run --cap-drop ALL`.

Since we pass the capabilities strings from K8s API to docker directly, K8s API also supports it. And there are user relying on this now:
https://github.com/microservices-demo/microservices-demo/blob/master/deploy/kubernetes/complete-demo.yaml#L24

The problems are:
1) Should we support this in K8s API? Since we've supported it so far, I doubt we could deprecate it.
2) Should we support this in Kubelet? This is a linux specific thing, but we are doing linux specific thing in Kubelet anyway.
3) Should we support this in container runtime?

Since it's code freeze, I don't think we could update K8s now. We'll support this in cri-containerd for now, and let's revisit this in 1.9.

/cc @ijc Thanks for finding this.
@yujuhong @feiskyer @tallclair @mrunalp 
/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-api-reviews 

---

> Should we support this in Kubelet? This is a linux specific thing, but we are doing linux specific thing in Kubelet anyway.

+1 for defining the default set of capabilities in the kubernetes codebase. kubelet should translate the kubernetes api to a set of capabilities and pass them to the runtime using CRI.

Yes, we should definitely support dropping all capabilities. I think we should define the api using `'*'` rather than `ALL`, since that's what we use elsewhere in the Kubernetes API (e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8823a835655cfcf73ddf8a636e2e11f83baeea57/pkg/apis/extensions/types.go#L889)

To clarify, we should carefully deprecate `ALL` (in favor of `*`) over a few releases to avoid breaking users.

title: CRI: Behavior of empty AppArmor profile is not clearly defined.
content:
For seccomp, we defined: ``` // Seccomp profile for the sandbox, candidate values are: // * docker/default: the default profile for the docker container runtime // * unconfined: unconfined profile, ie, no seccomp sandboxing // * localhost/: the profile installed on the node. // is the full path of the profile. // Default: "", which is identical with unconfined. ``` However for apparmor, we only defined: ``` // AppArmor profile for the container, candidate values are: // * runtime/default: equivalent to not specifying a profile. // * localhost/: profile loaded on the node // (localhost) by name. The possible profile names are detailed at // http://wiki.apparmor.net/index.php/AppArmor_Core_Policy_Reference ``` From the definition, it seems that empty apparmor profile will be "unconfined", because there is no other "unconfined" option. However, it is not the case today. When apparmor profile is empty, we'll return empty https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockershim/helpers.go#L203. However, in docker, it will apply `docker-default` if apparmor profile is empty, when apparmor is enabled on the OS. https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/6b262572028cc249b7da8cc55459197395fdb33e/daemon/oci_linux.go#L788-L792 IIUC, this means that, **as long as the node supports apparmor, `docker-default` will be applied to every pod, every container, no matter pod has apparmor label or not** Is this the behavior we want? @tallclair We should clearly define what is the expected behavior. @feiskyer @yujuhong @mrunalp @mikebrow /cc @kubernetes/sig-node-api-reviews --- Do you think it's reasonable to apply `docker-default` in dockershim? As it is docker specific. > * runtime/default: equivalent to not specifying a profile. @Random-Liu There is no unconfined AppArmor problem, default is `runtime/default`, whose behavior is defined by runtime itself. > Do you think it's reasonable to apply docker-default in dockershim? As it is docker specific. @resouer In dockershim, yes. but Random's main concern is the behavior of empty AppArmor profile. Agree with @feiskyer . The `runtime/default` is explicitly not defined at the Kubernetes level (hence the `runtime` prefix). For docker / containerd, this should be the docker-default profile. For everything else, it's up to the authors. As part of AppArmor graduating out of beta, we may want to consider defining a `kubernetes/default` profile (which would probably be identical to `docker-default` in practice). And if we had one how would you point the runtime to that profile or would you simply specify it in a doc somewhere and the runtimes would have to generate it? I sort of figured if it's not runtime/default, or localhost/profilename that it would be a path to a profile that's been configured for the container. But at the moment it's invalid of not runtime/default or localhost/profile, right? The way apparmor currently works, the runtime expects the profile to already be loaded (in the kernel), and just takes a name that references it. If we had a Kubernetes default profile, I would expect the Kubelet to load the profile, and pass the name to the runtime. > @resouer In dockershim, yes. but Random's main concern is the behavior of empty AppArmor profile. @tallclair It's still not clear to me what is the behavior for empty AppArmor profile. Today, even if user doesn't apply any apparmor label, default docker apparmor profile will be applied. Is this expected behavior? Mark 1.9. I think we should clearly define this in 1.9 @Random-Liu Yes that's the intended behavior. I think it would be reasonable to define a default Kubernetes profile though. > Today, even if user doesn't apply any apparmor label, default docker apparmor profile will be applied. Is this expected behavior? @tallclair, this seems misleading to me... Whether the default apparmor profile will be applied to containers or not become a node-level decision, and is hard to detect by the end users. Perhaps this should be a cluster-level setting? We can set the default for every pod automatically. Another question. Do we ever want to allow a container to run without any apparmor profile? This seems not doable today if apparmor is enabled on the node. Unfortunately AppArmor profiles aren't a cluster managed resource yet (I think they should be prior to AA going to GA). This means that it's hard to enforce anything at the cluster level. But for the ideal eventual state, I agree the defaulting should be done at the cluster level. @Random-Liu Thanks for raising the issue. It also confused me. The application I deployed requires AppArmorProfile specified as "unconfined" together with few extra capabilities. I could run "docker run --security-opt apparmor=unconfined --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN --cap-add=SYS_RESOURCE --cap-add=IPC_OWNER ..." to launch the application. However in Kuberentes, according to following doc, I have to run the Pod as privilege mode. I cannot specify AppArmorProfile as "unconfined" explicitly in Kubernetes. Any suggestion, I could specify AppArmorProfile as "unconfined", but don't have to run Pod in privilege mode? @luckyfengyong - Thanks for the report, that's a bug. title: update gcloud compute calls to remove --zones and --regexp
content:
As of `gcloud` 164.0.0 (2017-07-26), the `--zones` and `--regexp` flags are deprecated from a number of `gcloud compute` calls: * `gcloud compute disks list` * `gcloud compute disk-types list` * `gcloud compute instance-groups unmanaged list` * `gcloud compute instances list` * `gcloud compute machine-types list` * `gcloud compute target-instances list` We use these pretty extensively in our cluster scripts, and we need to update them to use `--filter` so they don't mysteriously break in the future. --- I'd like to take a look at this. It is my first kubernetes bug, so please let me know if there's anything I need to do apart from opening a PR referencing this issue number. Welcome! That should be all you need to do. I'd assign this issue to you, but GitHub doesn't allow assigning to non-org members, so your comment will have to suffice. Also leaving as a note: it looks like `gcloud` [165.0.0 (2017-08-02)](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/release-notes#16500_2017-08-02) deprecates `--regex` and `--regions` for: * `gcloud compute target-vpn-gateways list` * `gcloud compute target-pools list` * `gcloud compute vpn-tunnels list` * `gcloud compute commitments list` These don't appear to be used in the codebase, but worth noting for future reference. Please note that any of the changes need to be cherry-picked to earlier release branches also. Otherwise presubmit tests will fail for PRs on those branches (unless you skip e2e tests for those branches which I don't think we want). I think this issue is becoming increasingly important, as I've been asked by at least 3 people by now why the kube-up/kube-down scripts are failing. Could someone make sure it's fixed asap? gcloud 168.0.0 seems to have broken things further. I'm now consistently getting stuff like ``` ERROR: (gcloud.compute.instance-groups.managed.list-instances) wrong collection: expected [compute.regionInstanceGroupManagers,compute.instanceGroupManagers], got [compute.instanceGroups], for path [...] ``` Yes.. Heard the same issue from @jcbsmpsn too very recently. The fix needs to go in asap. this latest breakage seems different. `gcloud compute instance-groups managed list` is now returning a URL, and `gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances` isn't parsing that URL correctly. fyi - @wojtek-t @mwielgus This is being worked on by @pci in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/50398 Cherry pick PRs are https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/51651 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/51652 There's at least one call we missed because it used `-r` instead of `--regexp`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7e5d2df2995ef402a2e4ee39524c761904bf7689/cluster/gce/util.sh#L1835-L1838 Frustrating, but an easy fix. [MILESTONENOTIFIER] Milestone Labels **Complete** @ixdy Issue label settings: - sig/cluster-lifecycle: Issue will be escalated to these SIGs if needed. - priority/important-soon: Escalate to the issue owners and SIG owner; move out of milestone after several unsuccessful escalation attempts. - kind/cleanup: Adding tests, refactoring, fixing old bugs.
Additional instructions available here The commands available for adding these labels are documented here
> Also it's great how gcloud crashes, rather than handling the deprecation gracefully. Wonderful. Sorry we missed that one. Everything is terrible. Now we're getting warning messages like ```console $ nodes=$(gcloud compute instances list --project k8s-scale-testing '--filter=(metadata.created-by:*zones/us-east1-a/instanceGroupManagers/gke-cluster-1-default-pool-c9471aa4-grp)' '--format=get(name)') WARNING: --filter : operator evaluation is changing for consistency across Google APIs. metadata."created-by":*zones/us-east1-a/instanceGroupManagers/gke-cluster-1-default-pool-c9471aa4-grp currently matches but will not match in the near future. Run `gcloud topics filters` for details. ``` Had a quick look, the change was introduced in 168.0.0.0 (although there's nothing in the release notes!). [Here are the new docs](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/topic/filters) and `:` is now only allowed an optional _trailing_ `*`. Switching to `--filter=(metadata.created-by~'.*zones(..)'` should fix it, but I won't get a chance to test until the weekend. @ixdy says that this issue is not a release blocker for 1.8, but that we will need to backport the fix into the 1.8 release branch. @ixdy - I'm going to bump this out of the 1.8 milestone as it isn't a release blocking issue, but we shouldn't lose track of fixing it. Thanks @roberthbailey A new arrival in my family has meant I've not had time to get make a PR for this, if it's still here when I have some time I'll take it. title: Kubernetes API Server should not depend on --cloud-provider and --cloud-config
content:

> Uncomment only one, leave it on its own line:

/kind bug

**What happened**:
I was quite surprised to see `--cloud-config` and `--cloud-provider` in the api server when reviewing some code around openstack cloud provider. Turned out that this was needed by a single admission controller, namely `PersistentVolumeLabel`

@dims

cc @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs

Thanks @bgrant0607 @smarterclayton 

@smarterclayton @rrati Found it! looks like this one https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/44680

@dims Cool that you found it! I was just about to dig it up :)

cc @cheftako 

More work is being done in #51629

Also we should talk about if the SSH-to-nodes GCE thingy is really needed anymore with the latest auth features...
@kubernetes/sig-auth-feature-requests  

@luxas is that involved with the cloud provider? I was under the impression it was just flags on the API server that didn't interact with an external service.

```
      --ssh-keyfile string                                      If non-empty, use secure SSH proxy to the nodes, using this user keyfile
      --ssh-user string                                         If non-empty, use secure SSH proxy to the nodes, using this user name
```

@ericchiang Now remember, I was thinking about the node dialer talking to the cloud provider re: installing SSH keys: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L212-L241

Only provider that implements this `AddSSHKeyToAllInstances` function in the cloudprovider interface is GCE. I'm asking whether this is _actually_ required anymore or if we can deprecate and remove...

@luxas Do you mean removing the ssh tunnelling feature completly or just removing `AddSSHKeyToAllInstances` from the cloud interface?

I'd like to see the tunneling feature removed. If a particular deployment topology requires it, I would expect that deployment to set up VPN–style tunneling for specific IP ranges, rather than adding complexity throughout the API server

@liggitt Sorry to hear that. I was hoping to build on that feature in our deployment. Setting up vpn tunnels requires more outside machinery and complicates the setup considerably in my case.

The complication is there regardless of whether it is built into the api server or not, and the tunneling built into the api server is opaque, not as robust as dedicated vpn solutions, and has been repeatedly problematic. 

@liggitt that seems like a reasonable direction to explore, but needs more discussion, as this is currently supported functionality. Also concerned that this comment will get buried and missed in what was reported as a bug. 

@jagosan Anyway, it's only GCE that's using this. Removing GCE-only code in the core k8s codebase is a general theme anyway in my understanding. As @liggitt said, we don't strictly need this _in the core api server_.
On this note, kube-up.sh has been deprecated for a long time, and the plan is to move over to using kubeadm eventually. We will have to hack on the way GCE/GKE deploys clusters anyway. And, I'm not sure I see the exact value to have this now that we have better authn/authz mechanisms in core (as compared to before, where this was strictly needed)

Can we deprecate this functionality now, and work out a plan to stop using it in GCE/GKE gradually please?
We can definitely move this to a separate issue...

@luxas I am not against the idea, just making the point that this discussion has veered off topic and don't want important discussions to get lost when this issue (reported as a bug with a title that isn't obviously related to the dialer's continued existence) is somehow resolved. 

This is part of larger work - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48690

title: Local Storage Request/Limit Validation Discussion
content: ## Feature: local storage request/limit From v1.7, we add the feature to allow users set local storage limit for pod’s emptyDir and container’s writable layer (overlay) to better provide storage capacity isolation. For all type of resources in Kubernetes, user can set value for request and/or limit. The relationship between request and limit is defined as follows - A BestEffort quality of service is provided when a request and limit are not specified. - A Burstable quality of service is provided when a request is specified that is less than an optionally specified limit. - A Guaranteed quality of service is provided when a limit is specified that is equal to an optionally specified request. The quality of service has an impact on what happens if the resource is compressible or not. For incompressible resource such as memory, a BestEffort container will be able to consume as much resource as is available on the node. In addition, a BestEffort container has the greatest chance of being killed if there is an out of resource event on the node. A Burstable container will be scheduled on the node to get the amount of resource requested, but it may consume more. If there is an out of resource event on the node, containers of this type will be killed after BestEffort containers when attempting to reclaim resource. A Guaranteed container will get the amount of resource requested, but no more. In the event of a system out of resource event, it will only be killed if there are no more BestEffort or Burstable containers on the system. For Burstable container setting, one problem is that resource could be over-committed. The scheduler will tend to pack more Pods to the nodes. When disk is under pressure, the eviction manager will try to reclaim storage resource and evict pods to free up resource if reclaim is not enough. Storage is also an incompressible resource like memory. However, unlike memory, reclaim storage resource and free disk space take much longer time and incur more overhead. So the system would be much more stable if it can allocate enough resources for the workload at the first place to avoid reclaim. ## Proposal: request/limit validation One proposal is to enforce that request is always equal to limit for local storage. User will set a reasonable value for storage request/limit so that Pod gets enough disk space. In this way, the system will schedule the Pods to nodes where there is sufficient resource and also make sure Pods will not use more than requested to avoid over commitment. The reason behind this is that storage is relatively cheap. One future Vertical pod autoscaling can help reduce wastage. https://github.com/kgrygiel/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/vertical-pod-autoscaler.md The downside of this proposal is that for some very burstable workload, it might be difficult to set it a good value for request and limit. If the value is too big, it will waste resource. Otherwise, if the value is small, the pod might get evicted very easily. Open this issue for further discussion on how we should validate the local storage request/limit. Feedback is appreciated. --- /cc IIUC, storage request/limit is not counted when calculating Be, Bu, Gu, for mostly the same reason listed here. > For all type of resources in Kubernetes, user can set value for request and/or limit. title: Storage Allocatable does not take eviction thresholds into account
content:
Node Allocatable is calculated as `Capacity - kube-reserved - system-reserved - hard-eviction-thresholds`.
This is true for `memory`, but not true for `storage` though.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/46456 introduced `storage` support in node allocatable, but failed to include `hard eviction thresholds` [here](https://github.com/jingxu97/kubernetes/blob/943fc53bf727ff6e005378a872710071042abf72/pkg/kubelet/cm/node_container_manager.go#L218)

How does this affect users?

If a user set's `storage` as part of `kube-reserved` and/or `system-reserved` and set's `hard eviction thresholds` for `storage`, then their pods will get evicted even though the overall usage is within `allocatable`. Essentially nodes will get over committed from a storage standpoint.
This is not a v1.7 blocker because storage is not yet a production ready schedulable resource.

cc @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs @jingxu97 @saad-ali

title: e2e test the Node Authorizer
content:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?** (choose one):

TESTING REQUEST

Spawned from: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/46879
It would be nice with some e2e tests for the Node Authorizer so consumers of it (kubeadm, GCE, GKE, etc.) could easily make sure it's enabled and working, just by editing `ginkgo.focus` when running e2e's.

I wrote a quick bash script of what it could do:

```bash
if [[ $(kubectl version 2>&1 | grep "Client" | grep 'Minor:"7') == "" ]]; then
	echo "kubectl v1.7.0-beta.0 or higher is required"
	exit 1
fi

export KUBECONFIG=/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
IMPERSONATE="--as system:node:thegopher --as-group system:nodes"

printf "TESTING: Getting a non-existent secret should exit with the Forbidden error, not a NotFound error] "
([[ $(kubectl ${IMPERSONATE} get secret foo 2>&1 | grep "Forbidden") != "" ]] && printf "PASSED!\n") || printf "FAILED!\n"

printf "TESTING: Getting an existent secret should exit with the Forbidden error] "
([[ $(kubectl ${IMPERSONATE} get secret $(kubectl get secret | grep token | awk '{print $1}') 2>&1 | grep "Forbidden") != "" ]] && printf "PASSED!\n") || printf "FAILED!\n"

printf "TESTING: Getting a secret for a workload the node has access to should succeed] "
kubectl ${IMPERSONATE} -n kube-system get secrets $(kubectl -n kube-system get secret | grep kube-proxy | awk '{print $1}') 1>/dev/null 2>/dev/null
([[ $? == 0 ]] && printf "PASSED!\n") || printf "FAILED!\n"

printf "TESTING: A node shouldn't be able to create an other node] "
echo '{"apiVersion":"v1","kind":"Node","metadata":{"name":"foo"}}' | kubectl delete -f - 1>/dev/null 2>/dev/null
echo '{"apiVersion":"v1","kind":"Node","metadata":{"name":"foo"}}' | kubectl ${IMPERSONATE} --validate=false create -f - 1>/dev/null 2>/dev/null
([[ $? == 1 ]] && printf "PASSED!\n") || printf "FAILED!\n"
```

The bash script above is in no way comprehensive enough, but on the other hand it took  ~5mins to write :)

For now (1.7), we might use something like this bash script in our kubeadm e2e CI job to make sure the Node Authorizer/Admission plugin is enabled correctly.

cc @kubernetes/sig-cluster-lifecycle-feature-requests @kubernetes/sig-auth-feature-requests

title: Resource quota support for GPU resource
content:
**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`):
1.6.4 for both server and client

**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: GKE and On premise
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Debian Jessie and Ubuntu 16.04
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): 4.4.0-78 (ubuntu)
- **Install tools**: Managed service for GKE, Ansible for on premise

**What happened**:
When I define a resource quota limit with GPU resources in it to limit the number of GPU allocated to a namespace as  

```apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota
  namespace: test
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "12"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    requests.alpha.kubernetes.io/nvidia-gpu: "1"
    limits.cpu: "12"
    limits.memory: 8Gi
    limits.alpha.kubernetes.io/nvidia-gpu: "1"
    configmaps: "100"
    services: "100"
    secrets: "100"
```


It creates the `quota` object without any warning. But when I try to run any deployment in that namespace, I get the error as
 `Warning   FailedCreate   replicaset-controller   Error creating: pods "tensorflow-3620546736-" is forbidden: status unknown for quota: quota`. 
This error goes away if I remove the GPU from resource quota. Also looking at the [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/) it seems GPU is not supported for quota. 

**What you expected to happen**:
I expect that in the above quota case, user will be able to run workload in `test` namespace with 1 GPU at max.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
Apply the above quota to a namespace and try to deploy any deployment with or without GPU, you will see the error. 




---

@kubernetes/sig-apps-bugs @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs 

/assign

Nvidia GPUs is currently in `alpha` phase. Quota, defaulting, etc. will be handled as part of `beta`. The API will change from alpha to beta and so quota objects will not be ~~portable~~ forwards compatible even if they were to support GPUs today. 

@vishh I think its not only for GPU but in general quota resource should support [opaque resource](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#opaque-integer-resources-alpha-feature). As it is supported by accounting/scheduling in kubelet/scheduler. So it should be possible to limit the amount of those resource in the cluster per namespace.

@gurvindersingh We are planning on replacing the current opaque integer resource model with a more extensible one. That's one of the reasons why opaque integer resources are still in `alpha`. Expect a proposal on the new APIs with quota integration in the next couple of months. 

+1 to everything that @vishh stated.  i generally avoid quota on alpha resources at this time.

@vishh @derekwaynecarr That is understandable, I look forward to have the `beta`version of opaque resources with support for quota included. I assume that it will be target for 1.8

@vishh @cmluciano any update on this to get quota applied on GPU resources.

/cc

@gurvindersingh This will likely not land in a release until 1.9 (release date in December). 

This may take longer than v1.9. I'd like to introduce an extensible resources pipeline before adding quota for extended resources. The Resource type `alpha.kubernetes.io/nvidia-gpu` will be removed in v1.9 in favor of a new resource type.

Try creating a service with a cluster IP. Then try accessing the _service_ IP and port from within a target pod. It hangs. As far as I can tell, `SYN` but that is it.

Should be able to access the service from any pod, whether one of the targets or a different one.

---
kind: Deployment

  name: nginx
spec:

#### Working pod:
`exec` into any pod _other than_ the one created as part of the deployment:

1. `curl <nginx_podIP>:80`: works
2. `curl <nginx_serviceIP>:80`: works

#### Failing pod
`exec` into the pod created by the above deployment:

1. `curl <nginx_podIP>:80`: works
2. `curl localhost:80`: works
2. `curl <nginx_serviceIP>:80`: **FAILS**

**Anything else we need to know**:

It doesn't matter if you use the same port for the service as for the pod or a different one, same name or different name, etc.

This is why kubenet has been modularized and encapsulated over the last

The hairpin stuff was added to make pod-connecting-to-itself-via-a-service-IP work when using the iptables-based kube-proxy. It's possible that it also has the effect of fixing other things (pod-to-self-NodePort or whatever), but if so, then apparently those things were broken before and we didn't care that much.

Why should we allow plugins to not support this?

> Why should we allow plugins to not support this?

Because AFAIK there still are situations where hairpin can cause panics. But I am not the expert on it.

> > Why should we allow plugins to not support this?

Kernel `hairpin_mode` can cause panics, but the proposed rule wasn't "Plugins have to support kernel `hairpin_mode`", it was "Plugins have to support the use case 'a pod can connect to itself via a service IP' (somehow)". True. But do we want to make it too restrictive? Would we not want a more open approach that says, "you must support this or indicate clearly that you do not"?

In that case, you can release a network that does not support it, and let users decide if the trade-offs for a particular CNI plugin are worth it.
