title: Support scheduling tolerating workloads on NotReady Nodes
content:
This has come up a few times; right now the kubelet goes NotReady if the CNI network isn't set up which makes the scheduler not even consider scheduling to that node, not even hostNetwork Pods.

I think that it's in the works to mark Node problems with Taints, where are we with that effort @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-misc?

We should make it possible to schedule workloads on nodes that are NotReady **if the workload tolerates all the required taints for the specific condition**.
This is critical for kubeadm self-hosting for example.

I will add more context on this later, but starting the discussion at least here... didn't find any other issue although it may exist

@kubernetes/sig-node-feature-requests @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-feature-requests @kubernetes/sig-network-feature-requests 

---

/kind feature

@luxas The title is confusing. If a node is not reachable at all, why should scheduler schedule any pods on it and even if the scheduler does, how does the node know that it should run the pod? I can see how this may work if the node is not ready for reasons other than reachability though.

+1 to this, some customer want to use `host network` so do not have calico installed, and for this case, we should enable the pod can be created. Perhaps introducing a new taint for this to enable the pod can still be scheduled to the node even if calico is not running.

similar question with @bsalamat , is there any condition to identify "network" issues? If so, that'll be great to have such a feature.

+1 for this feature. For baremetal node, you probably will use host networking for the performance reasons. You would not want to cripple it with using overlay networking.

> @luxas The title is confusing. If a node is not reachable at all, why should scheduler schedule any pods on it and even if the scheduler does, how does the node know that it should run the pod? I can see how this may work if the node is not ready for reasons other than reachability though.

> similar question with @bsalamat , is there any condition to identify "network" issues? If so, that'll be great to have such a feature.

@bsalamat @k82cn Sorry for the confusion, was in a hurry when I wrote the issue description initially. This is not about connectivity, full connectivity is assumed at all times.

This is about nodes that have some known "problem" e.g. NetworkNotReady. That condition means that the node is reachable over the network but no CNI network (e.g. kubenet, Weave or Calico) is installed.

However, currently, when one of the five-ish node conditions that exist are falsy, the Node goes unschedulable due to the NodeNotReady condition. If one sub-condition (NetworkNotReady is true), the full node condition goes falsy.

We should be able to do more fine-grained scheduling than that. In the CNI networking case you might want to run some workloads (of type hostNetwork=true obviously) on nodes with no CNI network installed for bootstrapping or other reasons.

One possible solution (there are quite a few):
 - Make the kubelet create taints for all the falsy conditions it experiences
    - e.g. the kubelet will create the `node.alpha.kubernetes.io/networkNotReady` taint if the CNI network isn't initialized.
 - Enable scheduling on `NodeReady==ConditionFalse` nodes (behind a flag on the scheduler possibly to keep backwards-compability)
   - Or make it possible for "special" workloads to tolerate being scheduled to NotReady nodes in some way.


Example of the current state:
```
$ kubectl describe nodes
Name:			thegopher
Role:			
Labels:			beta.kubernetes.io/arch=amd64

Here is the code that probably should be changed in some way (`plugin/pkg/scheduler/factory/factory.go:475`):
```
func getNodeConditionPredicate() corelisters.NodeConditionPredicate {
	return func(node *v1.Node) bool {
		for i := range node.Status.Conditions {
			cond := &node.Status.Conditions[i]
			// We consider the node for scheduling only when its:
			// - NodeReady condition status is ConditionTrue,
			// - NodeOutOfDisk condition status is ConditionFalse,
			// - NodeNetworkUnavailable condition status is ConditionFalse.
			if cond.Type == v1.NodeReady && cond.Status != v1.ConditionTrue {
				glog.V(4).Infof("Ignoring node %v with %v condition status %v", node.Name, cond.Type, cond.Status)
				return false
			} else if cond.Type == v1.NodeOutOfDisk && cond.Status != v1.ConditionFalse {
				glog.V(4).Infof("Ignoring node %v with %v condition status %v", node.Name, cond.Type, cond.Status)
				return false
			} else if cond.Type == v1.NodeNetworkUnavailable && cond.Status != v1.ConditionFalse {
				glog.V(4).Infof("Ignoring node %v with %v condition status %v", node.Name, cond.Type, cond.Status)
				return false
			}
		}
		// Ignore nodes that are marked unschedulable
		if node.Spec.Unschedulable {
			glog.V(4).Infof("Ignoring node %v since it is unschedulable", node.Name)
			return false
		}
		return true
	}
}
```

cc @kubernetes/sig-cluster-lifecycle-bugs @kubernetes/sig-cluster-lifecycle-misc 

Currently we _could_ workaround this by using DaemonSets as they aren't using the default scheduler: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/42002
But that'd be a poor solution and will stop working in a future release.

xref : https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/42001

> Make the kubelet create taints for all the falsy conditions it experiences

Indeed someone is already working on this (#42406). Feel free to comment on that PR. I think there are some issues with it, for example it appears to be using one taint for everything instead of one taint per condition. I haven't had a chance to look at it.

> Enable scheduling on NodeReady==ConditionFalse nodes (behind a flag on the scheduler possibly to keep backwards-compability)

We should not hide behavior like this behind flags. If a pod wants to schedule on a node with NetworkNotReady taint, it should have an explicit toleration for it.


Just go through #42406 , it handled this case by taint for everything as davidopp said. Appended a comments in #42406 for this case.

@luxas , I think we should not mark `NodeReady` to `ConditionFalse` if `NodeNetworkUnavailable` is acceptable. IMO, if `NodeReady` is `False`, it means that node can not run any Pod event it tolerant everything, e.g. some internal critical issue of kubelet. 

slack with luxas, if do not mark `NodeReady` to `ConditionFalse`, that may introduce backward compatibility issue :).

`NodeReady = false` basically means that Kubelet is down or can't reach API server, which in turn means that there's no reason for tolerating NoSchedule Taint corresponding to it (as Kubelet won't notice your Pod either way). To my understanding conditions are supposed to be completely orthogonal, so state of the one, should not influence state of another. One can infer if the Node is "ready enough" by looking at all of them (and yes - there was pretty long discussion about it roughly 2 years ago @davidopp @bgrant0607).

That being said +1 to having separate Taints for each Condition.

The example for host-network=true can be leveraged with kubenet. Kubenet is not an official CNI plugin, but it works for the purpose that you mentioned. Does the noop plugin not work anymore - 

```
By default if no kubelet network plugin is specified, the noop plugin is used, which sets net/bridge/bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 to ensure simple configurations (like docker with a bridge) work correctly with the iptables proxy.
```

This issue (and #44445)  led @gmarek and me to realize that there is not a good understanding and agreement of what the actual and desired behavior is for node conditions (and for the taints that we want to replace them with for scheduling purposes) in general. Before we try to do anything, we need to take a step back and get this understanding. @gmarek and I started talking about all of the scenarios and it turns out that it's incredibly complicated.

Anyway, @gmarek filled a [spreadsheet](https://docs.google.com/a/google.com/spreadsheets/d/1nHOyGrs9oJoPOYOvk8hOQeqqASDk4H3UuW4pvpXKyaQ/edit?usp=sharing_eip&ts=591c70ee) which people should take a look at and make comments/corrections to. 

Oops, @gmarek is still working on the spreadsheet, so the link isn't public yet. @gmarek please post to this issue when it is ready to share. Sorry about that.


Sure - the doc is [here](https://docs.google.com/a/google.com/spreadsheets/d/1GT6XmdzG0TTmip0WH92mFQq84qcRn_oQUZ7Q2KFIjwQ/edit?usp=sharing)

IMO there is a conflation of "Conditions" with an implicit state vs. having an explicit state machine. This leads to the glue logic that exists in kubelet, and if we follow this track it would make it's way into the scheduler.  



> We should not hide behavior like this behind flags. If a pod wants to schedule on a node with NetworkNotReady taint, it should have an explicit toleration for it.

@davidopp I meant that the feature to _be able to take NotReady nodes into account_ could be added behind a feature flag for the scheduler possibly already in v1.7?
Of course the workload itself must tolerate everything in order to get scheduled...

> That being said +1 to having separate Taints for each Condition.

Great @gmarek, I think that's step number one

> NodeReady = false basically means that Kubelet is down or can't reach API server, which in turn means that there's no reason for tolerating NoSchedule Taint corresponding to it (as Kubelet won't notice your Pod either way).

@gmarek I thought that `NodeReady=ConditionFalse` meant that not every sub-condition is true; the kubelet experiences some problems. And that `NodeReady=ConditionUnknown` meant that the node isn't reachable by the control plane. Isn't that understanding right?

> IMO there is a conflation of "Conditions" with an implicit state vs. having an explicit state machine. This leads to the glue logic that exists in kubelet, and if we follow this track it would make it's way into the scheduler.

@timothysc I'm not sure I understand how this glue logic would make its way into the scheduler. There wouldn't be any new code added to the scheduler really, only proposal (from me, at least) is to allow taking `NodeReady=ConditionFalse` nodes into account. (still exclude the unreachable ones)

@luxas - my understanding is different. I think that all conditions are independent, and `NodeReady` is also independent of others, and it means that there's something fundamental wrong with the Node (I believe that it mostly means that runtime is down). I guess it's best to ask @kubernetes/sig-node-proposals 

>  I thought that NodeReady=ConditionFalse meant that not every sub-condition is true; the kubelet experiences some problems. And that NodeReady=ConditionUnknown meant that the node isn't reachable by the control plane. Isn't that understanding right?

Your description of ConditionUnknown is correct but not ConditionFalse. As @gmarek said the conditions are independent of one another, e.g. NodeReady can be false when NetworkUnavailable is false, or they can both be true, etc.

 > I meant that the feature to be able to take NotReady nodes into account could be added behind a feature flag for the scheduler possibly already in v1.7?

Sure, if you want to add a flag that defaults to "not enabled" that allows scheduling pods onto NotReady nodes I guess that's harmless. But I'm not sure that's what you actually want, given the misunderstanding about NotReady (i.e. that it is actually an independent condition)?

@luxas So we talked about this issue today in sig-scheduling.  There is not a plan of record to leverage taints and conditions.  The NetworkNotReady condition seems to be conflated with the NotReady status.  

It would be good to know when and how the node gets into the NotReady status and how exactly has that changed. 


BTW NetworkUnavailable has been around for a long time
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/26415


> There is not a plan of record to leverage taints and conditions.

Just to be clear - there IS work in progress to apply taints for these don't-schedule conditions but it is not going to make 1.7.


Possibly related  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/43815 ? 

More prior art: #34398, #33573, #33438

I'm bumping priority down now that I understand the context of where kubeadm self hosting is at.  


> Currently we could workaround this by using DaemonSets as they aren't using the default scheduler: #42002
> But that'd be a poor solution and will stop working in a future release.

Yeah, I think we need to fix this behavior before we change the DaemonSet controller to use the default scheduler.  Various CNI network providers (Calico, Flannel, Weave) rely on DaemonSets being able to schedule hostNetwork pods when `NetworkUnavailable` is true.

Another use case for this that we hear a lot is the ability to deploy networking via helm.  Helm requires the tiller pod to run on the cluster before being able to deploy any charts.  Given the current behavior this makes it impossible to deploy network daemonsets via helm.

Ah, this is even worse than I thought...

@timothysc 
> @luxas So we talked about this issue today in sig-scheduling. There is not a plan of record to leverage taints and conditions. The NetworkNotReady condition seems to be conflated with the NotReady status.
> It would be good to know when and how the node gets into the NotReady status and how exactly has that changed.

See: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L658
```go
var newNodeReadyCondition v1.NodeCondition
rs := append(kl.runtimeState.runtimeErrors(), kl.runtimeState.networkErrors()...)
if len(rs) == 0 {
	newNodeReadyCondition = v1.NodeCondition{
		Type:              v1.NodeReady,
		Status:            v1.ConditionTrue,
		Reason:            "KubeletReady",
		Message:           "kubelet is posting ready status",
		LastHeartbeatTime: currentTime,
	}
} else {
	newNodeReadyCondition = v1.NodeCondition{
		Type:              v1.NodeReady,
		Status:            v1.ConditionFalse,
		Reason:            "KubeletNotReady",
		Message:           strings.Join(rs, ","),
		LastHeartbeatTime: currentTime,
	}
}
```
I took for granted without even looking deeper at it that **NetworkReady** actually was a **Kubernetes Node** condition, but it isn't. It's a _CRI Condition_, which can't be used for scheduling.
What we have now is a blob in the **KubeletNotReady** condition that can fail for a number of different reasons.

I really think that the NetworkPluginNotReady CRI condition should be reported as a Node Condition as well instead of being baked into the general KubeletNotReady condition. Now we lack granularity in all kinds of ways. And we can't remove the NetworkPluginNotReady -> KubeletNotReady behavior anymore, since that's GA functionality now.

```
    - lastHeartbeatTime: 2017-05-30T13:06:04Z
      lastTransitionTime: 2017-05-30T13:05:04Z
      message: 'runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false reason:NetworkPluginNotReady
        message:docker: network plugin is not ready: cni config uninitialized'
      reason: KubeletNotReady
      status: "False"
      type: Ready
```

PTAL @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs. Is there any specific reason the CRI condition reporting was designed as-is?

> PTAL @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs. Is there any specific reason the CRI condition reporting was designed as-is?

Reporting unready network plugins as part of the node ready condition predated CRI. In fact, the logic was there at least on or before kubernetes 1.2, before taints/toleration was introduced.

I do think we should clarify/re-define the conditions and interactions with the control plane. 

I think this is bad, but I don't think it's release blocker bad.  

I do agree it's feature blocker bad for both "self-hosted" and daemonsets->scheduler.  

Does anyone have cycles to investigate?  

> I think this is bad, but I don't think it's release blocker bad.

@timothysc Totally agree. Won't affect the release since the behavior has existed a couple of releases already.

> I do agree it's feature blocker bad for both "self-hosted" and daemonsets->scheduler.
> Does anyone have cycles to investigate?

I might have some time, let's see how things turn out

> I do think we should clarify/re-define the conditions and interactions with the control plane.

@yujuhong Where should we have this conversation?

@luxas @yujuhong - there's an started work in #42406, that I didn't have time to properly drive. First step of cleaning up all this mess was gathering the data I shared in a trix. Next step is to decide what semantics we want to have (and which behavior we want to break), which I planned to do after the freeze (and after I dig myself out of stuff that accumulates during it).

@gmarek, thanks and looking forward to see the progress on this!

> @yujuhong Where should we have this conversation?

@luxas, it's unlikely that we'll have time to tackle this before the 1.7 release settles down. I think @gmarek's plan sounds great. 

cc @davidopp 

Any update on this? I just ran into this issue again.

there's an alpha feature in 1.9 (TaintNodeByCondition), please try it :).

I think we can close this as it's implemented in alpha and the feature tracking state is here: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/issues/382

What was the final result of this? I could not find documentation that said, "here is how you schedule a `Pod` on a node that has network not yet ready.

I _think_ the net result is that you:

1. enable tainting the node by condition
2. Add a toleration for the specific taint (in this case, network not being ready if you are using `hostnetwork`

But I am unsure. Is that correct? How do I enable them and what is the correct toleration? Is there an example?

@deitch i am also interested as I would like to deploy calico via a helm chart which would require this functionality.

@swade1987 It's already been implemented, the taint key is: `node.kubernetes.io/network-unavailable`

Last I looked, running tiller as a statefulset/deployment with net=host and the toleration still didn't let it schedule. maybe that has changed though?

For the record, this has worked for me with today's master (pre-1.11):

* Enabled feature gate `TaintNodesByCondition=true` everywhere
* Run a pod with toleration:
   ```
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod

     name: testpod

       - key: node.kubernetes.io/network-unavailable

   ```

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/taint-and-toleration/#taint-based-evictions

Could definitely be more clear. Not possible to find without knowing the name of the taint.

```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"6", GitVersion:"v1.6.2", GitCommit:"477efc3cbe6a7effca06bd1452fa356e2201e1ee", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2017-04-19T22:51:55Z", GoVersion:"go1.8.1", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"}

```


I was pleased to see the graduation of init-containers to GA.  Unfortunately, there are two problems with how k8s is dealing with them:

Our use case involves a Django application component.  The idea is to use init containers to deal with pre-flight checks and handle any pre-launch processing that needs to happen before the application comes online (typical use as per the docs)

Since these processes make use of the same image:version, it is necessary for the containers to run the same version of the app image.

Defining the init-containers in `.template.spec.initContainers` works with the initial deployment; however, any change to the deployment spec file within `.template.spec.initContainers` is not properly processed.   Any subsequent applications to the deployment will cause the *initial* init-container definitions to run, but, of course, they're running the wrong version.  This problem affects the entire init-container element definition, not just `image`.

Another interesting feature of this bug is that despite not having defined the init-containers in `.template.metadata.annotations`, the running deployment shows that the `.template.spec.initContainers` definitions have had their JSON equivalents packed into both `pod.alpha.kubernetes.io/init-containers` *and* `pod.beta.kubernetes.io/init-containers` annotations.

*NOTE*: At this point in my investigation, my original spec file has its init-containers defined only in `template.spec.initContainers`

At this point I'm thinking the API must be pre-processnig`template.spec.initContainers` to create the annotation strings--not a typical GA feature feature, but whatever... I'll roll with it, right?

I decided to convert the init-container defs to JSON and see if the deployment problem goes away.  

*NOTE*: At this point `.template.spec.InitContainers` is removed from the spec file

Defining and subsequently updating the init-containers as beta annotations work just like in 1.5.  Functionally, I'm in good shape; however, I ask the API for its view of the deployment spec and `.template.spec.initContainers` *is back*!  


**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**:
gce

- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release):
Debian 8


**What happened**:

see above

**What you expected to happen**:

I expected the support of the beta annotation to be the piece that was duct-taped onto the new spot on the API for init-containers rather than the other way around. 

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Create a deployment that uses a versioned image for an init-container with the definitions under `.template.spec.initContainers[]`

Once the deployment is verified to work, update the spec file's init-container definition to use a different version of the image.

After deployment, `kubectl describe deployment thing` and gaze in dismay.

Convert init-container definition to annotation JSON string.  Redeploy.  Functionally happy.



**Anything else we need to know**:

It appears part of this pig's lipstick is that when I either view or attempt to directly edit the deployment spec, the annotation is converted back into YAML for my viewing pleasure (with the alpha *and* beta init-container annotations in the template metadata).  If I try to delete said YAML, kube-api doesn't complain; however, another `kubectl get deployment -o yaml` shows the bits that I just deleted!  

Needless to say, if someone else comes along to interact with this deployment or its child pods, their first instinct will be to (try to) interact with the YAML structure, not the nightmarish JSON strings.  



---

Another observation: after creating a sparkly new deployment, the API returns a structure that includes the `.templates.spec.initContainers` bits even though the deployment spec file does not include one.

Whoever spent time making it look like this was done needs to be stared at balefully for at least a few minutes.


cc @smarterclayton

Made a simple digging into the code and found the root cause might be [here: SetInitContainersAndStatuses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e09fda63bea41a4b0ebceb2325c47d1f3c97ac90/pkg/kubelet/config/config.go#L264).

@smarterclayton would give a detailed explanation.

@erictune re beta annotations.

Unfortunately, part of supporting beta annotations is that they must override and take priority over the fields.  Otherwise they would break if someone set init annotations.  We will drop the annotations in 1.X (I was hoping 1.7, but not sure what guarantee we established, so 1.8 if not 1.7)

kubelets can skew two versions older than the apiserver, so 1.8, probably

/sig apps

That's all very interesting, but that doesn't mitigate init-containers being essentially broken in 1.6 (relative to the 1.6 documentation page)

To reiterate:

* defining init-containers using GA notation works for the initial deployment. 
  *  If any part of the GA notation is modified, subsequent deployments do not trigger an update
  * if any part of the GA notation is modified, subsequent deployments *must* involve _manual_ deletion of the _annotation strings_ before the GA notation-based modifications will trigger an update
  * if  init-containers are defined using annotation strings in the original deployment doc, the initial and subsequent deployment trigger updates as expected only if init-container configuration continues to be maintained via annotation strings

Following the above advice from @gladiatr72, we've tried to delete the init container annotations prior to new deploys and thought it might help someone facing the same issue. Our init containers don't change so frequently and we just started using them a bit more so we needed a workaround for these issues on k8s 1.6.4.

If we only delete the annotations, they seems to get restored immediately from the GA notation. At the point in time we wish to clear the init containers they reference the old versions. It seems the only way for us to update init containers on k8s 1.6.4 is to delete both the annotations and the GA notation:
```
✗ kubectl patch deployment --type=json <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> \
-p='[{"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.beta.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}, 
  {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.alpha.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"},
  {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/spec/initContainers"}]`

deployment "<DEPLOYMENT_NAME>" patched

✗ kubectl get deployment <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> -o yaml

<result does not have any init containers so ready to be updated>
```

To clarify, deleting only the annotations like this command below does not work for us because afterwards `DEPLOYMENT_NAME` still has the annotations and GA notation present despite kubectl saying it has been patched:
```
✗ kubectl patch deployment --type=json <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> \
-p='[{"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.beta.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}, 
  {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/metadata/annotations/pod.alpha.kubernetes.io~1init-containers"}}]`

deployment "<DEPLOYMENT_NAME>" patched

✗ kubectl get deployment <DEPLOYMENT_NAME> -o yaml

<result still has both alpha and beta init container annotations plus the GA notation>
```

the population of the annotations happens during conversion, and can be removed in 1.8 (since the oldest supported kubelets will be at 1.6, which recognizes the API fields)

@liggitt Thanks, understood. Looking forward to it! Hopefully the above can help someone needing a workaround before 1.8.

fixed by #51816

title: [Federation] Ingress should detect NodePort mistaches
content:
The documentation for federated ingress [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-federation/ingress/#adding-backend-services-and-pods) says:

> Note that in order for your federated ingress to work correctly on Google Cloud, the node ports of all of the underlying cluster-local services need to be identical. If you’re using a federated service this is easy to do. Simply pick a node port that is not already being used in any of your clusters, and add that to the spec of your federated service. If you do not specify a node port for your federated service, each cluster will choose it’s own node port for its cluster-local shard of the service, and these will probably end up being different, which is not what you want.

For services with non-matching nodeports, we should be generating events for mismatching NodePorts instead of following through with the ingress creation.

---

@csbell Should this be blocking 1.7?

No, it's a "nice to have", won't make it.

There are two ways to make this better:

1. Make the federation control plane smart enough to select an unused nodeport across all clusters.
2. Until the above is in place, fail attempts to create federated services with unspecified nodeports.

I think that the workaround above is good enough for GA.

This issue was labelled only for sig/multicluster and is thus moved over to kubernetes/federation#135.
If this does not seem to be right, please reopen this and notify us @kubernetes/sig-multicluster-misc.
/close

title: Upgrade to Go 1.8. resulted in significant performance regression
content:
Since:
https://k8s-gubernator.appspot.com/build/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-kubemark-gce-scale/394
kubemark-scale started consistently failing.

It seems that some metrics are a bit higher (though this doesn't seem to be the problem).

The main problem is that now all the runs are timing out. I looked into logs from few runs and the pattern seems to be exactly the same in all of them:

- the phase between "Creating services" and "Services created" in load test is now ~2x longer.

I looked into PRs that were merged at that time and there is only one PR that may be related:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/41636 [bump Go to 1.8.1]

As a short term fix, I'm going to extend timeout of the kubemark-scale job, but we need to understand why this happened - this may potentially be a blocker for Go 1.8.

@k8s-mirror-scalability-bugs @luxas @ixdy @timothysc @smarterclayton @gmarek @shyamjvs 

---

Are we certain proxy updates have not occurred in that window?  

> Are we certain proxy updates have not occurred in that window?

I don't understand. But I'm pretty sure. Everything else takes exactly the same amount of time except from this one (and this is increase from ~30m to~1h) so it's not negligible.

The full list of changes between runs 393 and 394: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/fb72285a7...508041e9d

@ixdy - yes, I've already went through it. The only potential change is golang update.

BTW - this regression is not visible at all in kubemark-500.

Just to clarify what I was saying about, before regression:
```
I0425 17:14:00.185] Apr 25 17:14:00.185: INFO: Creating services
I0425 17:34:16.206] Apr 25 17:34:16.205: INFO: 16400 Services created.
```
After regression:
```
I0504 09:47:05.513] May  4 09:47:05.513: INFO: Creating services
I0504 10:50:29.462] May  4 10:50:29.461: INFO: 16400 Services created.
```

These are coming from those 2 runs:
https://k8s-gubernator.appspot.com/build/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-kubemark-gce-scale/393?log#log
https://k8s-gubernator.appspot.com/build/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-kubemark-gce-scale/406?log#log

The difference is ~3x

So it seems that it is really related to Go.

I didn't yet to final analysis of this, but I grabbed some profile from kubemark-5000 and we are spending majority of time in Go-related stuff - see the following profile as an example:

[out.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/979021/out.pdf)

In particular, I'm seeing ~40% in runtime.selectgo, and ~50% in futex

@bradfitz - any thoughts on it?

We may be forced to revert back to go 1.7.5 once we have final confirmation.
@ixdy @bradfitz @jessfraz @wojtek-t @timothysc @spxtr @thockin @smarterclayton @bprashanth @gmarek

@wojtek-t I hope we could try to investigate it as long as possible and try to fix it either on the k8s side (if some Go semantics has changed and we need to update it to preserve behavior) or on the Go side by using a newer 1.8 patch version if something was wrong but easily-fixable in the runtime

@wojtek-t 

- Do you see any backup on the clients?  
- What do the memory and cpu traces look like between the two runs?  

On 1st blush the changelog for 1.8 has some suspicious items: https://golang.org/doc/go1.8#more_context 

/cc @jeremyeder fyi. 

@wojtek-t, do you have a version of that out.pdf from before the switch to 1.8.x? I'd like to look for differences.

@timothysc, the optional http2 push stuff doesn't worry about me. That was a pretty small optional addition off to the side of existing http2 code. The most notable part there was that we made the decision to expose it all the way through to the main net/http package. But if you're not using it, you should be using roughly the same code. The more interesting list of http changes is https://golang.org/doc/go1.8#net_http



@bradfitz sorry I meant the items below that point.
More Context Support
Mutex Contention Profiling 
...

@timothysc, I don't think those are involved here and I see no evidence they are.

> @wojtek-t, do you have a version of that out.pdf from before the switch to 1.8.x? I'd like to look for differences

I don't. But I'm almost sure it that those futex and runtime.selecgo wasn't that significat before (which suggest golang scheduler?).
Anyway - to avoid guessing, I will try to grab those profiles on Monday from both 1.7.5 and 1.8.1 versions.

So after some issues that I faced, I managed to produce a comparison for profiles. And now I can confirm with 100% confidence that the regression is because of Go upgrade.

So basically, I've run 5000-node kubemark cluster (from head) and run load test on it (just did first 15 minutes or so of it - it's enough).

At head (with Go 1.8.1):
- apiserver is pretty consistently using ~36 cores (all the time without spikes etc.)
- ~30s after starting tests, the profile looks like:
[go_18_begin.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/983992/go_18_begin.pdf)
- ~10m after starting tests, the profile looks like:
[go_18_10min.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/983993/go_18_10min.pdf)

Then I:
- reverted #41636 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/44961
- apiserver is using ~12-13 cores, with spikes to 20-25 cores (I guess this is because of GC)
- ~30s after starting tests, the profile looks like:
[go_17_begin.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/984006/go_17_begin.pdf)
- ~10m after starting tests, the profile looks like:
[go_17_10min.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/984010/go_17_10min.pdf)


It's pretty clear that this regressions is because of Go. maybe we are doing some non-optimal things, but the change is huuuuge.

@brandfitz - can you please take a look?

1.8 : 
```
net/http.(*http2serverConn).serve
1.49s(0.19%)
of 458.83s(57.03%)
```
Stands out like a sore thumb vs. 
```
net/http.(*http2serverConn).serve
0.43s(0.27%)
of 10.60s(6.60%)
```

I'm busy with OSCON this week. Maybe @tombergan can take a look.

Do you have a self-contained `func BenchmarkFoo(b *testing.B)` we can run locally? Firing up 5,000 nodes is a little painful of a repro.

Or, do you know which HTTP handlers exhibit the most throughput decrease and what their write characteristics are so we can try to write a similar ServeHTTP benchmark func? Is the `k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/metrics.(*fancyResponseWriterDelegator).Flush` flushing relevant perhaps?

We don't have any benchmark.

I'm not Go expert, but my feeling is that it's not about any particular handler that was slower. Looking into profiles, it seems that http2serverConn is slower, as @timothysc pointed above:

Go 1.7: net/http.(*http2serverConn).serve: 6.6%

Go 1.8: net/http.(*http2serverConn).serve: 57.03%
(out of which 96% going into runtime.selectgo)

It seems that either something in http2serverConn became slower or goruntime scheduler got slower.

The http2 server code did grow 3 more select cases between 1.7 and 1.8:

```patch
@@ -3406,8 +3548,10 @@ func (sc *http2serverConn) serve() {
        for {
                loopNum++
                select {
-               case wm := <-sc.wantWriteFrameCh:
-                       sc.writeFrame(wm)
+               case wr := <-sc.wantWriteFrameCh:
+                       sc.writeFrame(wr)
+               case spr := <-sc.wantStartPushCh:
+                       sc.startPush(spr)
                case res := <-sc.wroteFrameCh:
                        sc.wroteFrame(res)
                case res := <-sc.readFrameCh:
@@ -3424,12 +3568,22 @@ func (sc *http2serverConn) serve() {
                case <-settingsTimer.C:
                        sc.logf("timeout waiting for SETTINGS frames from %v", sc.conn.RemoteAddr())
                        return
+               case <-gracefulShutdownCh:
+                       gracefulShutdownCh = nil
+                       sc.startGracefulShutdown()
                case <-sc.shutdownTimerCh:
                        sc.vlogf("GOAWAY close timer fired; closing conn from %v", sc.conn.RemoteAddr())
                        return
+               case <-sc.idleTimerCh:
+                       sc.vlogf("connection is idle")
+                       sc.goAway(http2ErrCodeNo)
                case fn := <-sc.testHookCh:
                        fn(loopNum)
                }
+
+               if sc.inGoAway && sc.curOpenStreams() == 0 && !sc.needToSendGoAway && !sc.writingFrame {
+                       return
+               }
        }
 }
 
```

Could you try locally deleting those three new ones (wantStartPush, gracefulShutdownCh, and idleTimerCh) and re-measure?

That would at least tell us whether it's select getting wider vs. the runtime itself being slower at select?

But it might be easier for us to test locally rather than spinning up 5,000 VMs. I just don't really have time this week.

If that is the case, fixing it is possible in x/net/http2 (which Kubernetes can explicitly import and use if you'd like) but this isn't really backport-worthy by our normal guidelines for point release cherry-picks.

I wish you would've found this during the Go 1.8 beta testing period.

Heads up that Go 1.9 is now code-frozen and you might want to start testing it already while we can still make changes. It will be shipped & frozen around August 1st.

> Could you try locally deleting those three new ones (wantStartPush, gracefulShutdownCh, and idleTimerCh) and re-measure?

How can I do it? Is it part of Godeps?

> But it might be easier for us to test locally rather than spinning up 5,000 VMs. I just don't really have time this week.

It's kubemark - so it is spinning 82 VMs (still takes time, but much easier than 5000 VMs). I can send more detailed instructions tomorrow if needed.

> How can I do it? Is it part of Godeps?

I don't work on Kubernetes and don't use Godeps, so I can't help you there. You'd need to patch the standard library, but I'm not sure how you get the standard library (or binaries) for building your Docker images before they're pushed to GCR (presumably?). I'm not familiar with any of that process.

> It's kubemark - so it is spinning 82 VMs (still takes time, but much easier than 5000 VMs). I can send more detailed instructions tomorrow if needed.

Well, I'm gone Tue-Fri, so no rush. But any instructions should also tell me how to patch in local changes.

> I don't work on Kubernetes and don't use Godeps, so I can't help you there. You'd need to patch the standard library, but I'm not sure how you get the standard library (or binaries) for building your Docker images before they're pushed to GCR (presumably?). I'm not familiar with any of that process.

I checked and it's not part of Godeps - we have some somehow automatically pull them in.

@timothysc @thockin @jbeda - do you know we can do this?

You can patch the golang installation in the crossbuild image and then use that to build kubernetes. We've done this before for other reasons, e.g.  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/aa045f786e424e787bd17d6bb564f5aa311dd7b0

@ixdy - thanks a lot! Will try to do that tomorrow.

It seems that I managed to build my own image - will see if what @bradfitz suggested above (cutting off these 3 new cases) helps with our performance.
For the reference, I built my own image from this patch:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...wojtek-t:debug_go_regression?expand=1

But further updates from me tomorrow.

This would also be a great time to try out tip (what will be Go 1.9); the select implementation changed since 1.8. And bugs or issues you find could be fixed as part of the release.

I ran the http2 package's `BenchmarkServerGets` a few different ways:

* with current tip code ("before") vs. tip code with the three new select cases removed ("after")
* with Go 1.8 vs tip ("Go 1.9")
* 1 simple response vs 100 flushed responses

With Go 1.9, for 100 flushed body chunks:

```

With Go 1.8, the same two are much more pronounced:

name          old alloc/op   new alloc/op   delta

It's nice to see that Go 1.9's handling of selects is improved, though. Thanks, @mdempsky.


I've run the tests that @bradfitz suggested.
Basically, I've used this PR:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...wojtek-t:debug_go_regression?expand=1
[we're patching one single file in net/http package]

and with that change we're back to be good (profiles from the same moments as the ones described above);
[go_18_patched_begin.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/986452/go_18_patched_begin.pdf)
[go_18_patched_10min.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/986453/go_18_patched_10min.pdf)

So as of now, we exactly understand where the problem is (the problem is not in goruntime implementation, but in new cases in select in net/http implementation).

Now the question is how we can fix this problem.
@bradfitz - is doing such patch for Go in 1.8.1 when building Kubernetes safe?
Can we solve this problem somehow in Go itself (ideally by patching Go 1.8.1)?
Maybe you can see some other solutions to it that we can have?

If neither of those is doable, our only option seems to be revert to Go 1.7.5.

> is doing such patch for Go in 1.8.1 when building Kubernetes safe?

I can't speak for if a such patch is safe to do, but it's very doable from our side as you saw from the commit, we've built a few releases with patched Golang GOROOT's already with great success for arm and ppc64le.

> If that is the case, fixing it is possible in x/net/http2 (which Kubernetes can explicitly import and use if you'd like) but this isn't really backport-worthy by our normal guidelines for point release cherry-picks.

I think what @bradfitz suggested here might be the best thing to do initially. Fix it in https://godoc.org/golang.org/x/net/http2 or in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/third_party/forked/golang/net/http possibly and do a `s|net/http|k8s.io/kubernetes/third_party/forked/golang/net/http|g` replace across the codebase.

The best solution from our side would be a go1.8.2 release, but not sure it meets the criterias, probably not.

Depending on how things turn out, the second best alternative would be vendoring https://godoc.org/golang.org/x/net/http2 (with the patch) and importing that as `net/http` everywhere.

If we can't do that, we maybe can add the patched package to `third_party/forked/golang` and re-import things from there.

And lastly we have patching the golang GOROOT inside the build container. This will give us official releases of that GOROOT, but folks can obviously bypass the build container and use plain go1.8 if they compile themselves, which might be troublesome.

As pointed out in https://groups.google.com/d/msg/kubernetes-dev/0XRRz6UhhTM/ms685QYdAAAJ, there might be some features that require go1.8, and if we have to revert (which I really hope we don't have to), those features might stop working.

cc @pipejakob @mikedanese ^

> @wojtek-t: I've run the tests that @bradfitz suggested. Basically, I've used this PR:
> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...wojtek-t:debug_go_regression?expand=1
> and with that change we're back to be good. So as of now, we exactly understand where the problem is (the problem is not in goruntime implementation, but in new cases in select in net/http implementation).

I hadn't realized the select implementation might be O(n) on each call -- [actually it looks worse than O(n)](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/release-branch.go1.8/src/runtime/select.go#L278) -- although that makes sense in retrospect. I can think of at least two possible improvements:

1. The select implementation [has a comment](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/runtime/select.go#L225) that it does not optimize for the nil channel case. But the [http2 serve loop](https://github.com/golang/net/blob/master/http2/server.go#L765) might have at least 3 nil channels in the common case: settingsTimer.C (nil'd early in the connection), sc.idleTimerCh (only if an idle timeout was configured), and sc.testHookCh (only in tests). Optimizing select to ignore nil channels with a single-value recv might have the same effect as removing the cases.

2. We can merge cases. We have three timer channels, all of which could be merged if we manually sort the timers by earliest-to-fire and select on that channel only. We may be able to merge the first 5 select cases (wantWriteFrameCh, wantStartPushCh, wroteFrameCh, readFrameCh, and bodyReadCh) in some way, though I haven't thought through the details.

> Is it possible to run the benchmark at tip without the above patch to see if the bottleneck is entirely eliminated with the new select implementation

curl -sSL https://github.com/golang/go/archive/go${K8S_PATCHED_GOLANG_VERSION}.tar.gz | tar -xz -C ${K8S_PATCHED_GOROOT} --strip-components=1
```
to gather go source to compile against it.

Yes, although I doubt that sorting the cases is the source of the slowdown. :)

@wojtek-t can you create new CPU profiles, but add the `-lines` argument to `go tool pprof`, so that we can see where inside select the time is being spent? That might help eliminate a bunch of guessing. (If you have the old binaries and profiles around, you can use them again.)

That comment only applies if all but one case is nil. Is that common in this code?

> We have three timer channels, all of which could be merged if we manually sort the timers by earliest-to-fire and select on that channel only.

Note that timer-based channels are handled differently than other kinds of channels and might easily have very different performance characteristics. Probably not. I suggest we understand the problem a little more deeply before worrying about what nature the fix will take.

title: Design Proposal: Federated Job: Cross-cluster task rebalancing
content:
Figure out how best to do task rebalancing across clusters for Federated Jobs.

See #36197 for background.

@jianhuiz leads this effort.  Assigning myself as proxy, as he is not part of the K8s org yet. 

@kubernetes/sig-federation-feature-requests 

---

From @jianhuiz 

1. how to decide a re-balancing is needed (succeeded ==0 and failed >0? failed = 0 and active ==0 for a while?; active is far less than parallelism?; jobs on a cluster can succeed but significantly slower than other clusters)
2. how to make an efficient re-balance. should the succeeded count being considered when re-planning?

From: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TZ4ZMZ8AEOlVyK6H_q-zNpAdlzTip8sxMQUVQeQ-O-w/edit#

@David Oppenheimer
My understanding is that what's wanted here is "considered all nodes and it
can't schedule onto any of them"? We do surface that in PodStatus today in
PodReasonUnschedulable. In terms of how the federated job controller can
make use of this information without having to track each pod, I think the
missing piece is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/32863.
Once that's implemented, this kind of information should be surfaced in the
JobStatus, so the federated job controller only needs to watch the
per-cluster Jobs, which IIUC it is doing anyway. Until
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/32863 is implemented, I
think you would just have to periodically fetch the list of pending pods
from the underlying cluster, extract the ones that are unschedulable (by
examining PodReasonUnschedulable), find which of them were created by a
local instance of a federated Job, and then take action based on that.

@quinton-hoole 
I think a possibly sensible approach here might be to start by creating Jobs in the underlying clusters with only a single worker, and incrementally scaling them up (possibly one worker at a time) only once it has been demonstrated that workers are able to schedule in that cluster. That way, workers will be allocated to the clusters where they are actually able to schedule. Cluster-level Jobs that end up with a single pending pod will remain in that state (approximately) until either additional capacity becomes available, or the required workers are successfully scheduled into other clusters.

/close

title: Federated Ingress fails at high loads
content:
I filed an issue with some debugging information and details in the Ingress repo -  https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress/issues/645. I am also filing it to here to track federated ingress flakiness. This is critical and is blocking us from making federation presubmits "required" for all PRs.

@csbell assigning it to you for triaging.

/assign @csbell 

/priority failing-test

/sig federation

cc @kubernetes/sig-federation-bugs 

---

https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress/issues/645 was mostly about surfacing the hidden errors and turned out that was not sufficient to debug the issue.  It also turns out https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress/pull/652 wasn't sufficient to fix the underlying issue. 


@nicksardo has a new hypothesis that explains the reason behind this bug at high loads pretty well. I am just writing down his hypothesis here. 


Let's assume that we have 3 federated clusters and a Federated Ingress object `foo.` The current design of the Federated Ingress controller picks one of the 3 clusters as the leader cluster and propagates the Ingress object `foo`, to this leader cluster. It then depends on the Cluster Ingress controller (GLBC) in the leader cluster to allocate GCP L7 resources and update the status/annotations on leader cluster's version of `foo`. Federated Ingress controller then copies that status/annotations to the Federated Ingress object and propagates that to the remaining clusters.


GLBC, on the other hand, garbage collects (GCs) the GCP resources that aren't used anymore. GLBC runs the GC cycle at the end of every sync loop. Since there are 3 clusters in federation with independent GLBCs that share the same Ingress UID, they operate on the same set of GCP L7 resources. 


At high loads, sync loops run often and hence also GC resources frequently. Since we elect a leader cluster and wait for the GCP resources to be created by that cluster's controller, the controllers in other clusters that don't know anything about the Ingress associated with these GCP resources yet try to GC those resources. This leads to a deadlock where the leader cluster never succeeds in creating the load balancer as the resources get garbage collected by the other clusters.

@nicksardo has proposed a two-pronged approach to solve this problem

1. In GLBC, move the GC cycle out of the sync loop and instead run it periodically, once every 10 or 15 minutes.
2. Dramatically simplify Federated Ingress controller by eliminating the leader election logic and just propagating Ingress resources to all the underlying clusters simultaneously. This works because all the Ingress controllers in the underlying clusters create GCP resources using the same name since they share the same UID and these create operations are idempotent. Even if there are propagation or processing delays in one of the clusters, they should all eventually reach a stable state. Only caveat is to ensure that the ingress UID configmaps are synced across the clusters before the first Ingress object is propagated to the clusters.

This has a nice side effect in that this makes Federated Ingress controller look similar to other federated controllers.

cc @csbell 

@madhusudancs @csbell @nicksardo 

1. As far as I recall the cluster's GLBC's only share the same UID because the Federated Ingress Controller chooses one of their UID's (via the described leader election), and propagates it to the other clusters, hence I don't think that 2 above works?
2. Why not just fix the GLBC garbage collection logic.  It seems that's the root cause of the problem (i.e. GLBC deletes LB's that are still in use by other clusters).  Can you make GLBC aware that other clusters are still using the LB, and hence prevent it from garbage collecting it? That seems both simple and effective.

Or am I missing something here?


> As far as I recall the cluster's GLBC's only share the same UID because the Federated Ingress Controller chooses one of their UID's (via the described leader election), and propagates it to the other clusters, hence I don't think that 2 above works?

Federated Ingress unifies the UIDs using a leader election logic. I am sorry, my fault, I should have probably clarified that. UID unification will still continue to use the same logic. But that logic is not required for syncing Ingress objects. Once the UIDs are unified, Ingress objects can be simply copied to all the clusters simultaneously without the need for leader election.

> Why not just fix the GLBC garbage collection logic. It seems that's the root cause of the problem (i.e. GLBC deletes LB's that are still in use by other clusters). Can you make GLBC aware that other clusters are still using the LB, and hence prevent it from garbage collecting it? That seems both simple and effective.

We have talked about this and @csbell has some ideas around ref-counting but it is not clear how to implement that using the current GCP APIs, esp. we do not know if it possible to do concurrency control of L7 resources. As a side note: GCS allows such concurrency control on the storage buckets and objects.


> Can you make GLBC aware that other clusters are still using the LB, and hence prevent it from garbage collecting it? That seems both simple and effective.

@quinton-hoole also, any ideas around how to make that possible are welcome.

1. A UID will still be chosen and propagated to the other clusters - that's unavoidable. But this can happen well before any ingress objects are created. The UID is also being moved to the service controller so GCP internal and L7 LBs can share instance groups. 

2.  Making the GLBC aware of other clusters would probably mean adding state to configmap or doing something really ugly like putting state in resource Description fields. In my opinion, it's simpler to program the GLBC to handle existing resources and add cluster-specific backends where necessary.


@madhusudancs @csbell @nicksardo 
Yes, a few ideas:

1. I don't know what you mean by "concurrency control of L7 resources" but I think at most all you need is optimistic concurrency (e.g. version ID's, like in Kubernetes), to prevent two API clients (in this case GLBC's) from trampling on each other.
2. Beyond that, I think it might be even easier than that, potentially.  Each GLBC can see what IP's are behind the LB.  If only it's own clusters IP's are there, then no other cluster is using the LB, and it can be deleted. You will need to do something to avoid the obvious race condition there, but that seems doable (e.g. using a lock resource on the GCE API).

@nicksardo @madhusudancs @csbell It's probably worth having an in-person discussion about this, as I really don't understand all the above arguments, and it will probably be quicker to resolve this with a quick discussion.  Call me any time on my cell if you need to.

> I don't know what you mean by "concurrency control of L7 resources" but I think at most all you need is optimistic concurrency (e.g. version ID's, like in Kubernetes), to prevent two API clients (in this case GLBC's) from trampling on each other.

That's what I mean. What are those version ID's that could be compared-and-swapped using GCP APIs?

 > Beyond that, I think it might be even easier than that, potentially. Each GLBC can see what IP's are behind the LB. If only it's own clusters IP's are there, then no other cluster is using the LB, and it can be deleted. You will need to do something to avoid the obvious race condition there, but that seems doable (e.g. using a lock resource on the GCE API).

I am not entirely sure what you mean here. Also, not sure what you mean by using a lock resource. Where would that be stored?



@quinton-hoole 
The ingress GC logic will be changing and get smarter - that's a given. But with the 7 different types of resources and the introduction of the service-controller sharing resources with the GLBC (same region), these changes may or may not be trivial. The first priority will be to decrease the frequency of GC - it's achievable and most likely make this a non-issue.

My second point is that we're not sure we need to let a single GLBC create LB resources before others.  If federated ingress sends out the object to all clusters, n-1 clusters could fail on the first sync, but be fine on the next. This task is not necessary to make federated ingress stable, sorry if it came off that way.  

@madhusudancs Should this issue be blocking 1.7?

No.

This issue was labelled only for sig/multicluster and is thus moved over to kubernetes/federation#131.
If this does not seem to be right, please reopen this and notify us @kubernetes/sig-multicluster-misc.
/close

title: K8s/CNI Plugin Compatibility
content:
This issue is mainly for discussion and tracking for cni integration related problems. CNI spec is somehow open-ended. Kubelet/Dockershim provides cni network plugin to integrate with 3rd-party cni plugins. 

**Requirements and Limitations**

- CNI spec only specifies 2 verbs, ADD and DEL. There is no LIST or GET operation to retrieve states. This implies that Kubelet/Dockershim must memorize the state and supply correct cni parameters for ADD/DEL.

- For setup, kubelet calls RunPodSandbox and dockershim triggers ADD using user provided cni net config. Kubelet only utilized cni plugin in a limited way:
  * Only the first valid network config from `cni-config-dir` is picked. This will change in the future as multi-network gets implemented. 
  * The result response from cni plugin is not really used.
  * Pod IP is retrieved by nsenter into the pod's netns. 

- Kubelet calls StopPodSandbox which triggers cni DEL at multiple occasions asynchronously.
  * If user deletes pod. 
  * If current pod sandbox did not match the desire state.
  * If any unwanted pod was presented.
  * Kubelet container GC will call StopPodSandbox and make sure it return successfully before continue to RemovePodSandbox. This is to make sure all resources have been released. 

- Dockershim maintains checkpoint per pod sandbox. This helps dockershim to store necessary information to recover and clean up after unexpected disruption (e.g docker/kubelet/dockershim crash, pod sandbox missing). Checkpoint is removed at the very end in RemovePodSandbox. As long as checkpoint exists, kubelet assumes that sandbox and its allocated resource are not removed completely.

**Problems (Feel free to add more)** 
- Some cni plugin return error on duplicate DELs (even with empty CNI_NETNS). Hence Container GC could not proceed to RemovePodSandbox and leave pod in Terminating status. Or even worse case, pod is gone, but container GC could not complete successfully. Hence leaving more and more checkpoints. 
- In the case of recreating pod sandbox, some cni plugins are dependent on the execution sequence of ADD/DEL for the same pod. 

**Proposed Solution**
1) Require cni plugins to tolerate duplicate DELs (at least with empty CNI_NETNS). Put this in CNI spec. 
2) Ensure kubelet only triggers one successful StopPodSandbox per sandbox.
3) Ensure dockershim only triggers one successful CNI DEL per sandbox.


**Future work**
- Conformance test suite for 3rd-party cni plugins and net configs.

@kubernetes/sig-network-misc 









---

In order to tail logs from pods generated by a job until completion I run the following command:

This automatically stopped tailing when the pod stopped. Since upgrading our GKE server this hangs indefinitely. It's something on the cluster side, because using the same 1.6.0 version of kubectl against a 1.5.6 GKE cluster stops as soon as the job is done.

title: Support for GPUs in Kubernetes
content:
This issue is meant to track all issues and features around managing GPUs in kubernetes. This issue is meant to reflect priorities, timeline and owners too.
## v1.7
- [x] All GPUs get exposed to privileged containers #46007 [Owner: @cmluciano, Reviewer: @vishh ]
  - kubernetes/kubernetes.github.io#3870
- [x] Enable GPU node e2e tests - Requires starting VMs in GCE with GPUs [ Owner: @vishh  ] #45430
- [x] Enable Cluster e2e tests - Requires automated installation of Nvidia drivers on COS image [ @vishh] #45136

## Post v1.7 (1.8)
- [ ] Avoid depending of docker APIs for identifying GPUs in Use. Fixing this issue will make GPU integration work with all runtimes #43240 [Owner: @jiayingz, Reviewer: @vishh ]
- [ ] Add GPU metrics to cadvisor
- [ ] Run GPU e2e on PRs #47192

## Known Bugs
- [ ] Support for hot-plug of GPUs #44080 (Dropped because Nvidia drivers recommend rebooting nodes post installation)
- [x] gpusInUse info error when kubelet restarts #46087



---

I'd like to add [NVML support](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/414) to this list 

I'm also working on some of the [TODOs in the NVIDIA pkg](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/43240)

@cmluciano I'd prefer not tackling NVML until the overall integration for GPUs is finalized. Meanwhile, we can address all other open issues and improve testing, etc. 

xref: #44552

I prepared a proposal for what we call the [Container Device Interface (CDI)](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/545): A generic way to allocate devices, including GPUs, to containers.

----

We use Kubernetes to schedule scientific 3D visualisation applications onto a cluster. Hence our containers use GPUs / DRM and other device nodes (e.g. TTYs).  Scheduling of Pods to Nodes with a capacity for such devices can be dealt with using [Opaque Integer Resources (OIR)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#opaque-integer-resources-alpha-feature), where scripts external to Kubernetes handle device discovery and capacity reporting (see e.g. [kube-gpu-resources](https://github.com/urzds/kube-gpu-resources)).  The [Container Runtime Interface (CRI)](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/container-runtime-interface.md) already supports [binding host device nodes](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/api/v1alpha1/runtime/api.proto#L586) to a container.  What is currently missing is a way for the Kubelet to generically allocate the available devices of a certain type to a container while it is being started.  The Container Device Interface (CDI) shall bridge this gap.

----

Please find the [full text of the proposal](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/545) in our copy of the Kubernetes proposal documents.  We would love to hear feedback from the community on this proposal.

@therc Ahh. In that case I'd recommend waiting. I hope to define a beta API for Nvidia GPUs in v1.8.

/remove-priority P1

(I'm not actually sure this is the right priority, just trying to remove the old priority/PN labels)

The Documentation mentions that currently no GPU sharing is supported. We are strongly interested in having this as a feature. Is there an Issue tracking progress in implementing GPU sharing support?

https://github.com/fabric8io/kubernetes-model/blob/master/vendor/k8s.io/kubernetes/docs/proposals/gpu-support.md mentions this as a feature of GPU Support "v1" ("Support fractional resources so multiple pods can share the same GPU") any estimates when this might happen (or where it is tracked)?

I don't believe that this is a feature that we are targeting since I am not aware of wide-spread support of shared cards. cc @flx42 @renaudwastaken 

All Nvidia cards support sharing. Some (=recent ones) better than others. We have been sharing them for the past three years in our environment and for more than an year under Kubernetes, starting from G2 (Kepler-class) instances. There's an undocumented hack in pre-1.6 versions, but with recent ones you need ugly patching.
I brought it up in the past, but it's already difficult enough to find an agreement on more basic stuff like discovery. It is doable, but you'd need to bring a lot more state and GPU awareness into the Kubernetes scheduler (or use a separate one).

I also mentioned this before, but I'll re-iterate: there is no enforced isolation between computation kernels on the GPU. You should share the hardware only if you know what you are doing and/or trust what you are running.

By default, kernels from different processes can't run on one GPU **simultaneously** (concurrency but not parallelism), they are time sliced. The Pascal architecture brings instruction-level preemption instead of block-level preemption, but context switches are not free.
Also, there is no way of partitioning GPU resources (SMs, memory), or even assignin priorities when sharing a card.

I agree with @therc that there is higher priority work before considering GPU sharing.

For our usecase (multiple different Neural networks being evaluated in different containers) all the restrictions you stated would be fine. For us a very basic support in the form of stating how much GPU memory a Container needs (statically if needed) and scheduling to GPUs which still have enough "unclaimed" memory.
We don't need any form of enforcement of constraints or security on the GPUs themself.

Currently GPU sharing is possible with nvidia-docker and I would love to see basic support in Kubernetes (even manual management would be fine as a first step)

@vishh I would like to give a try about adding gpu metrics to cAdvisor. I commited a pr [43934](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/43934) in leveraging the nvidia-smi binary but it seems not a perfect choice depending of nvidia-smi. Do you think it's ok to leverage NVML instead of depending of nvidia-smi binary?

@tianshapjq the discussion for cadvisor is now here: https://github.com/google/cadvisor/issues/1436

I listed multiple options, but we haven't decided on which approach to follow.

@flx42 thx for your reference, I followed that issue as well. But I just wanna know if any news about this discussion?

Not that I'm aware of.

A couple comments related to future work:

1) Volta added more fine-grained sharing targeted at cloud companies. Perhaps the sharing should wait until that's adopted more.

2) Nvidia stated at their last conference nvidia-docker is being deprecated and they're making a newer version that doesn't rely on docker. Not sure if this changes anything.

@flx42 @shaklee3 I am wondering if you have more information about Nvidia's plan about nvidia-docker not replying on docker for the new version?

> 2. Nvidia stated at their last conference nvidia-docker is being deprecated and they're making a newer version that doesn't rely on docker. Not sure if this changes anything.

That could be interesting. I am wondering if more I could know more details about it?

We will need more details on the sharing semantics.

> Nvidia stated at their last conference nvidia-docker is being deprecated and they're making a newer version that doesn't rely on docker. Not sure if this changes anything.

Kubernetes doesn't really need nvidia docker since it has enough extensions to help surface nvidia GPUs to containers. We may have more than one way of handling Nvidia GPUs with Kubernetes though for a while, where libnvidia-container will be one of the solutions for a subset of users. The user facing APIs will remain the same though.

title: Federated tests should retry NodePort allocation
content:
In order to support running tests in parallel, we added randomized NodePort selection.  There appears to be some evidence that this is not sufficient and is causing e2e test flakes:

https://k8s-gubernator.appspot.com/build/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-federation/2510

```
I0331 20:31:25.848] I0401 03:24:49.018147       1 servicecontroller.go:580] Service 'e2e-tests-federated-ingress-fpnqr/federated-ingress-service' is not found in cluster federation-e2e-gce-us-central1-a, trying to create new
I0331 20:31:25.849] I0401 03:24:49.025434       1 servicecontroller.go:587] Failed to create Service "federated-ingress-service" is invalid: spec.ports[0].nodePort: Invalid value: 32589: provided port is already allocated
```

---

Hi, 
As a need contributor, I'm interesting of solving this issue.

I already check the current code, and propose to retry the service creation until success or all possible ports (between FederatedSvcNodePortFirst and FederatedSvcNodePortLast) have been tried.

If this approach is fine for you, I can submit a PR soon.

How do you plan to check if the NodePorts are available? In our presubmit test environment, tests run across many instances of federation control planes in parallel, but share the same underlying clusters. So this approach might be viable depending on how and where you plan to check for these used NodePorts.

my approach for getting an available port is a "Dummy" approach: create a list of possible available port, get one of them randomly, then try to create the Service. If Service creation failed. try to use another possible available port, until service creation success or all possible available ports have been tested.

Sounds reasonable to me. Go for it.

A couple of caveats: 
1. No need to create a real list, you could just use the range boundaries. 
2. Be careful about service creation failure. You need to check if the service shard creation failed in the underlying clusters and rollback all those shards before retrying.

@madhusudancs thanks for the caveats, I will do soon a PR.

title: Tag e2e tests for alpha features as such and exclude them as appropriate from upgrade testing
content:
Currently, there is no explicit tagging of e2e tests that exercise alpha features. Because we provide no guarantees for compatibility across k8s versions for these features, these tests frequently fail in our upgrade jobs when running some form of version-skewed testing (i.e. create a 1.5 cluster, upgrade the master to 1.6, run 1.5 E2E tests against the cluster).

We should tag any e2e tests for alpha features as such, and explicitly exclude these from the relevant upgrade test jobs to eliminate noise in the release cycles.  This will require ongoing maintenance to adjust the tags on the tests as a feature moves from alpha to beta to GA.

cc @timothysc @ethernetdan @marun

---

Some of the root causes around failures in some of the upgrade tests were breaking compat behavior from Alpha-Beta.  Perhaps it would be easier to just skip [Alpha] tests as part of upgrade, b/c we make no guarantees across releases.?.? 

/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-bugs @derekwaynecarr 

+1
There are alpha features known to be incompatible. If we see failures caused by such incompatibilities, we should skip the upgrade tests. The question is that "can we find a solution, such as versioning, etc., to automatically or semi-automatically detect these incompatibilities?" By semi-automatically I mean something along the lines of tagging all the tests with the features that they test. This needs to be done once. Then we can have a master config which lists all the features. We can mark which features we expect to break in the latest upgrade. We may want to have multiple of these master configs, each for upgrading from a specific version to another. The benefit of this is that we won't need to tag tests again and again for every upgrade.
Of course, all of these are just raw ideas that came to my mind as I was typing this message. If you think there is value, we can explore this more.

> The question is that "can we find a solution, such as versioning, etc., to automatically or semi-automatically detect these incompatibilities?" 

yes, just add [Alpha] to tests the exercise alpha features and add it to the ginkgo skip list.  

> yes, just add [Alpha] to tests the exercise alpha features and add it to the ginkgo skip list.

Sure, but as skriss said, that would require ongoing maintenance to adjust the tags in the future.

As long as it makes it into the general alpha => beta checklist, it seems pretty manageable.

I don't see why we can't add this logic in 1.7.  

I think manually tagging is fine.

But I am not sure alpha always implies we break compatibility. It just means we MIGHT break compatibility.
For example, 1.5 affinity test would work against 1.6 cluster, except for the fact that we flag-gated the 1.5 behavior in 1.6 and disabled it by default, which for some other features in the future (especially ones that are not using annotations in alpha) we might not do.

So I would suggest the tag say something more specific than just "alpha" -- it should imply alpha and not expected to work in next version.


> But I am not sure alpha always implies we break compatibility. It just means we MIGHT break compatibility.

It means we guarantee nothing so the tests should not be trusted outside of a release.  I think minimizing false positives on upgrade tests is our primary goal.

---

adding to the milestone for triage

> adding to the milestone for triage

Even if it's in 1.6, it also existed in 1.5.  I don't think it should block 1.6.

@ash2k does minikube try to launch a single go process which contains both the kube-apiserver and the kube-controller-manager?  That appears to be the most likely way for something like this to happen.  Kube isn't very well structured to do that given the accidental interaction via the global API registry which kube only tests in separate processes.

Yeah, that looks like what is being done here: https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/blob/69c85e98288361cd84d6d023b4a61b6829efb8c6/cmd/localkube/cmd/start.go#L109-L114 and here https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/blob/ceb25dfd43a1c9d4ab6e11fdc34fa4333cab4626/pkg/localkube/apiserver.go#L61 .

I don't think this is a kube problem.  It looks like a wiring problem for someone vendoring kube.  Removing milestone.

@deads2k Thanks for looking into it! Sorry, I have no idea how minikube works internally. If Kubernetes is not affected by this issue then it is not that bad. I was afraid to try my code on our real cluster and preventing it from starting up next time. However this is a serious inconvenience for minikube users.

> Even if it's in 1.6, it also existed in 1.5. I don't think it should block 1.6.

@deads2k 

I do not follow this logic. Why we do not need to fix this if the bug also exists for 1.5?

A crasher in 1.5.3 by definition is not a release blocker (since it already exists in a released version). The statement wasn't that we shouldn't fix it, just that it's not a release blocker

Can I ask whether this is something likely to be fixed as a bugfix in the k8s 1.5.X and 1.6.X branches?  If not, do I understand the suggestion above by @deads2k to be that minikube needs to run separate processes for those two goroutines and then all should work in both 1.5 and 1.6?

@donspaulding I agree with your interpretation of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/43430#issuecomment-288184931. The suggestion seems to be that this should not occur in a real k8s cluster. Do you happen to have a small reproduction case that I could try out? The one in the original post above seems to point to a live, moving repo.

I think the smallest repro case I've seen so far is the one @r2d4 put together in [this comment on minikube issue #1252](https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/issues/1252#issuecomment-295370860).  

I think this comes from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/44507, also https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/39816

TPRs never get registered with RegisterGroup (should they?), and the garbage collector controller as well as the namespace controller both use static RESTMapping, rather than a dynamic one.  The versions get enabled and registered, but the group does not get registered causing the panic here: 

https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/apimachinery/registered/registered.go#L285

When I registered the group TPR, the panics disappear since the controllers know about the mappings, however the garbage collector complains since it doesn't know how to garbage collect the TPR.  Right now the garbage collector suppresses some TPR errors https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/42862

One other possible fix is to ignore enable versions which don't map to a corresponding GroupMeta.  Probably not a great solution, but would fix this problem for us until we get dynamic RESTMappings in the garbage and namespace controllers 

Not super familiar with this part of k8s so feel free to correct me or point me in the right direction.  

FYI I couldn't reproduce this in a full cluster (without minikube) on GCE with a method similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/issues/1252#issuecomment-295370860. I brought up the cluster, created the TPR, then "upgraded" the master to the same version, which removes and recreates the master VM while keeping the data volume intact.

The TPR is still there, and I don't see any panics. This seems to support the hypothesis that the crash only occurs because of the unusual way minikube combines multiple processes.

@r2d4 Does it make sense to you that your proposed fix would be unnecessary for the full cluster case? Or is there something else I should try to reproduce?

I wasn't able to reproduce it on a local non-minikube cluster either.  The full cluster case does run into a similar issue, but is specifically ignoring the error here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/42862.  I don't think that the proposed PR is much different, but I understand if we want to keep it out of this repo.

#42862 has to deal with unknown restmappings because it is looking them up based on user input which could be completely bogus. 

The proposed PR for this issue is masking inconsistently registered internal groups and versions for TPR objects. We should fix the inconsistency by removing the version registration, not mask it (per @deads2k's comment)

Thanks for the clarification.  I'll update the PR to remove the version registration.

title: Role/ClusterRole creation doesn't cross authorizers nicely
content:
In order to create an RBAC role, I need to have all of the permissions that exist in the role, *through RBAC*. It doesn't matter If I have all the permissions through another authorizer.

On GKE, for example, if I want to use my Google identity to create a role, I first have to create an RBAC RoleBinding giving myself the `cluster-admin` role, even if I am the owner of the project that has the GKE cluster.

We should authorize role creation in a way that allows "super users" from other authorizers to use RBAC.

---

Cc @kubernetes/sig-auth-feature-requests 

As a workaround, a GKE cluster admin can grant themselves RBAC permissions first:
```
kubectl create clusterrolebinding i-am-root --clusterrole=cluster-admin --user=<myusername>
```

Another check like this? https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/39383

I was thinking something similar to that.

Strawman:
To see if a user should be able to create/update a clusterRole:
Check "clusterRoleBindings" "bind" on the root of the cluster.
To see if a user should be able to create/update a role:
Check "roleBindings" "bind" on the whole namespace.

If you can bind to any existing role/clusterRole, then you can create/update roles/clusterRoles.

I think this is reasonable if you assume there is always a superuser role in every context. It might fall over if you consider a namespace that only has some low privilege roles that you are now able to escalate.
